sens: That which provokes fear, dread
An event or a miracle that fills one with anguish
G5400.detail:
1. The word literally designates that which causes fright, that which inspires terror. It is a concrete thing or a visible event that elicits an intense fear reaction in the one who sees it. In Luke 21:11, Jesus uses it to speak of earthquakes, famines, and terrifying signs that will precede the end times: tangible realities that terrify.

2. More broadly, it is an extraordinary phenomenon, a miracle or a supernatural event that destabilizes and terrifies witnesses. The word emphasizes less the nature of the phenomenon than the impression it produces: only its terrifying, distressing character and its ability to deeply shake are retained.
G5400.origine: The word comes from the root φοβέω (phobeô), which means "to fear," "to be afraid." The suffix -τρον (-tron) indicates that which performs or produces the action: φόβητρον is literally "that which causes fear." It is a classical Greek term that appears in ancient Greek authors to designate terrifying things or miracles that inspire dread. The word is rare in the Bible: it appears only once in the New Testament.
G5400.emploi: The word φόβητρον appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 21:11, in the context of Jesus' prophetic discourse about the end times. Jesus lists a series of disasters—earthquakes, plagues, famines—referring to them as "terrifying phenomena" that will accompany the last days. In this eschatological context, the word does not refer to ordinary phenomena, but to extraordinary, miraculous, or catastrophic events that inspire visceral fear. This unique usage shows how the Christian tradition has adopted an expression from classical Greek to express the terrifying dimension of the signs of the end of the world.
G5400.portee: This word reminds the reader that the eschatological times will be marked by frightening and extraordinary events. It invites us to take Jesus' warnings seriously and not to fall asleep in indifference: the signs of the times are meant to awaken our vigilance and our expectation of the Lord's return. For the believer, recognizing these terrifying phenomena is to acknowledge that history is moving toward its fulfillment according to God's plan.

sens: Intense fear, dread before what threatens or surprises
Respect mixed with apprehension towards an authority or power
Religious reverence, deep respect towards God
Respectful caution in moral life and relationships
Terror, physical trembling before danger or a supernatural event
G5401.detail:
1. Fear is primarily concrete fear: that which the disciples feel when they see Jesus walking on the sea and think they see a ghost (Matthew 14:26). It is also the dread that miracles provoke (Luke 5:26: "filled with fear, they said: We have seen strange things today"). This fear seizes the entire body; it becomes terror.
2. Fear can be respectful towards an authority: when one fears magistrates, it is because one recognizes their power (Romans 13:3). It is the caution of one who knows there are consequences to their actions.
3. But above all, for the Bible, fear is the attitude of the heart before God—not a servile fear, but a reverence, a deep religious respect (Acts 9:31: "Fear seized everyone"). It is "the fear of the Lord," which is the beginning of all wisdom.
4. This reverence produces a just and reserved way of living (1 Peter 3:2: "when they see your chaste and respectful conduct"). It guides human relationships, as with servants towards their masters (Ephesians 6:5).
5. Fear often includes physical trembling (Romans 3:18 speaks of those who do not have the fear of God). It marks the whole being before that which surpasses man.
G5401.origine: The Greek word phobos comes from a root that evokes fleeing, retreating before danger. In Hebrew, it primarily translates "yirah" (יִרְאָה), which denotes fear in a broad sense—fear, but also respect and reverence. The Hebrew word has a double meaning: it can mean to fear an enemy, but also to "fear God" with veneration. The Greek phobos captures this dual richness. It is a common word in daily life (fear of an authority) and in religious life (fear of God).
G5401.emploi: The word appears 43 times in the New Testament. The Gospels primarily use it to describe human reactions to the miracles of Jesus: the disciples are afraid when they see Him walking on the sea (Matthew 14:26), people tremble in fear when they see His works (Luke 5:26). Acts shows the fear that grips the young Church in the face of the things of God (Acts 2:43). Paul uses it to speak of the relationship to God (Romans 3:18, 8:15) and to exhort slaves and servants to obey with fear (Ephesians 6:5). First John places it at the heart of faith: a mature faith casts out servile fear (1 John 4:18). The word sometimes denotes natural fear, often religious reverence, and in certain contexts, the fear of divine judgment.
G5401.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites us to distinguish between two forms of fear. There is the fear that must be rejected—that of doubt and separation from God (2 Timothy 1:7, 1 John 4:18). And there is the fear to cultivate—that which honors God, inspires respect for His holiness, and directs towards obedience. This "fear of the Lord" is not a paralyzing servitude, but a heart that trembles and bows before divine majesty, finding in it security and wisdom.

sens: Christian woman who held the office of deaconess
Person in whom Paul had confidence for an important mission
G5402.detail: Phoebe is a Christian woman mentioned only once in the Bible, in Romans 16:1. She is presented as a deaconess of the Church of Cenchreae, a port in ancient Greece: she therefore had a recognized responsibility in the service of the local Church. The title of deaconess shows that she was not a mere passive member, but someone who actively engaged in serving other Christians. Paul warmly commends her to the believers in Rome, indicating that he fully trusted her to represent his message and carry his letter: she was a woman of responsibility and spiritual influence in the early Churches.
G5402.origine: The name Phoebe comes from Greek and literally means "bright" or "shining like the sun." In Greek mythology, Phoebe was a name associated with Apollo and light. It is not a particularly common name in early Christian sources: it is encountered only here in the New Testament.
G5402.emploi: Phoebe appears only once in the Bible, in Romans 16:1. Paul introduces her as "our sister"—the expression shows that she is a respected and cherished member of the Christian community—and as "deaconess of the Church of Cenchreae." This role likely involved her helping the poor, the sick, and the needy, and playing a role in welcoming and assisting Christian travelers. Paul asks the Romans to receive her well, suggesting that she was going to Rome for an important reason, perhaps to deliver Paul's letter to the Churches in Rome.
G5402.portee: Phoebe reminds believers that women have always played an active and recognized role in the service of the Church. She shows that Christian commitment is not a matter of appearance or status, but of faithfulness and dedication to service. For each person, she poses the question: do I have the same confidence in my responsibilities that an apostle could have in Phoebe? How can I serve in my Church with the integrity she demonstrated?

sens: coastal region of the Mediterranean Levant, north of Judea
land inhabited by renowned merchants and sailors
G5403.detail: 1. Phoenicia is a coastal region of the Levant, located north of the land of Israel, along the Mediterranean Sea. It includes the port cities of Tyre and Sidon, famous for their maritime trade (Acts 21:2: a ship "was making its way to Phoenicia"). 2. Its inhabitants, the Phoenicians, were world-renowned merchants and sailors. In Acts, Christians scattered by persecution take refuge in Phoenicia and proclaim the Gospel to the Jews there (Acts 11:19: "went as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch"). 3. Phoenicia also represents a natural stop on the journey between Jerusalem and other lands, as shown by Paul who "continues his journey through Phoenicia and Samaria" while reporting to the apostles about the conversion of the Gentiles (Acts 15:3).
G5403.origine: The name "Phoenicia" comes from the Greek φοινίκη (phoinikē), which literally means "land of purple" (φοῖνιξ, phoenix = purple), because this region was famous in antiquity for the production and trade of purple dye, a valuable dye extracted from the murex. The term specifically refers to the Levantine coast, between present-day Syria and northern Palestine.
G5403.emploi: The word appears three times in Acts, always in the context of Christian preaching journeys in the early Church. In Acts 11:19, the disciples scattered by persecution flee there and proclaim the Gospel. In Acts 15:3, Paul and Barnabas pass through it on their way back from their first mission. In Acts 21:2, Paul boards a ship there. Phoenicia thus emerges as an early area of Christian expansion and a geographical crossroads of apostolic journeys.
G5403.portee: Phoenicia reminds us that the Gospel spread rapidly beyond the borders of Israel, reaching neighboring regions and communities of Jews in the diaspora. It also illustrates how God used trade routes and maritime paths for His word to be proclaimed throughout the Mediterranean basin.

sens: The tropical tree that produces dates, with its tall trunk and wide fan-shaped leaves
The branches or leaves of this tree, used as a symbol of victory and joy
G5404.detail:
1. The palm is the characteristic tree of the hot and arid regions of the Middle East. It produces dates, precious fruits, and its long green leaves form a crown at the top of the trunk. In Egypt, Judea, and Arabia, it was one of the most useful and revered trees.
2. In the Bible, its branches are used to express joyful acclaim and triumph. During Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, the crowd "took branches of palm trees" to greet Him (John 12:13), an act reminiscent of victory celebrations. In the vision of Revelation, the great heavenly multitude holds palms in their hands before the throne, symbolizing ultimate victory and eternal joy (Revelation 7:9).
G5404.origine: The Greek word φοῖνιξ likely comes from Phoenician and refers to both the tree and its reddish color. It translates the Hebrew תָּמָר (tamar), whose primary meaning is the tree in general and particularly the palm. The word retains this dual meaning: the tree itself and its fruits or branches.
G5404.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In John 12:13, it refers to the branches cut during Jesus' triumphant entry into Jerusalem, an event that Christian liturgy has commemorated long after. In Revelation 7:9, the term evokes the palms held by the elect in heaven, symbolizing their final victory. These two uses place the palm in a context of celebration, victory, and praise.
G5404.portee: The palm reminds the reader that Jesus' victory is not primarily military but spiritual. The heavenly palms teach that true victory belongs to those who persevere in faith and are clothed in the righteousness of Christ. It is an invitation to see beyond visible appearances and to rejoice in a victory that the world cannot give or take away.

sens: Port of Crete
G5405.detail: 1. Phoenix is a port located on the island of Crete, in the Mediterranean. It is a naval anchorage oriented towards the southwest and northwest, more favorable than another port for wintering.
G5405.origine: The name Phoenix (Φοῖνιξ in Greek) is of Phoenician origin. It may be related to Phoenicia, the historical region of the Levant from which the Phoenicians, great navigators and merchants of antiquity, came. The same Greek word could also refer to the date palm, a symbol of fertility among Mediterranean peoples.
G5405.emploi: Phoenix appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:12, in the account of Paul's journey to Rome. The ship carrying Paul as a prisoner, after leaving Crete, encounters bad weather and must seek a winter harbor. The sailors and the centurion decide to head towards Phoenix, known to be a better anchorage than the one they are in. This port represents a refuge sought during a dangerous sea crossing.

sens: one who kills a human being
one who commits voluntary homicide
one who takes life with malicious intent
G5406.detail: 1. A murderer is primarily simply one who kills a man: in Matthew 22:7, the king sends his troops to destroy the murderers, those who have committed the act of killing. 2. But the word especially designates one who kills voluntarily, with moral guilt: in Acts 3:14, the Jews ask for the release of a murderer instead of Jesus, which shows that the murderer is guilty of a serious crime. 3. The murderer is also one whose act reveals deep malice: in Revelation 21:8, murderers are listed among the sinners who will have their part in the lake of fire, alongside idolaters and liars, linking murder to rebellion against God. 4. The word can also qualify one who has shed blood unjustly: in Acts 7:52, Stephen tells the Jews that they have been the murderers of the Righteous, meaning they have killed one who did not deserve to die.
G5406.origine: The Greek word phoneus comes from phonos (murder, homicide), which designates the act of killing. This root evokes the idea of violence, of destruction of life. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the word often corresponds to retsakh or related terms that designate murder as a serious violation of divine law.
G5406.emploi: The word murderer appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly to designate men guilty of serious crimes. In Matthew 22:7, it refers to those who have committed murders. In Acts 3:14, Paul applies it to the criminal released in place of Jesus. In Acts 7:52, Stephen uses it to accuse the Jews of having killed the prophets and Jesus himself. In Acts 28:4, the barbarians think Paul is a murderer because divine justice punishes him. In 1 Peter 4:15, Peter warns against the risk of suffering as a murderer. In Revelation 21:8 and 22:15, the murderer appears in the lists of the reprobate excluded from the kingdom of God.
G5406.portee: This word reminds the reader that murder is a serious transgression in the eyes of God, inseparable from sin and rebellion against Him. It invites every believer to examine their heart: beyond physical murder, Jesus teaches that anger and hatred towards a brother are also a form of spiritual murder. By placing murderers among those excluded from heaven, Scripture affirms the absolute holiness of God and the ultimate seriousness of the commandment: you shall not murder.

sens: To take someone's life, to put to death
To commit murder, to violate the divine commandment
To destroy, to annihilate (in a figurative sense)
G5407.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to take the life of a human being. It is the act of putting someone to death, whether judicial or criminal. The text states, "whoever kills will be liable to judgment" (Matthew 5:21), which shows that it is the physical act of causing death.
2. From the commandment "You shall not murder" (Matthew 19:18, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20), the word designates the act of transgressing a fundamental divine law. It is a major sin: Jesus cites it among the essential commandments alongside theft and perjury. The Pharisees "have killed" the prophets (Matthew 23:31), meaning they have made themselves guilty of the crime of murder.
3. The word can also signify moral or spiritual destruction. James speaks of one who kills his brother (James 5:6), in connection with manifest injustice, which broadens its scope: it is to annihilate someone through violence or malice.
G5407.origine: The word comes from the root φόνος (phonos), which denotes murder and bloodshed. In ancient Hebrew, it regularly translates the verb רָצַח (ratzach), which also expresses the act of killing, particularly in the commandment "You shall not murder" from the Decalogue (Exodus 20:13). This Hebrew root primarily evokes the action of striking, breaking, and then causing death violently and illegally.
G5407.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the New Testament, almost exclusively to quote or comment on the commandment "You shall not murder." Jesus himself refers to it in Matthew 5:21, 19:18, as do Mark and Luke (10:19, 18:20), and Paul mentions it in Romans 13:9 as an imperative moral obligation. James uses it twice: in 2:11, where he reminds that violating this commandment is to transgress the entire Law, and in 4:2, where he asks where murders come from (in the context of conflicts and desires). Matthew 23:31-35 criticizes the Pharisees who "have killed the prophets," serious historical and spiritual accusations. The context is always grave: it concerns sin or crime against human life.
G5407.portee: This verb reminds every Christian of one of the most fundamental commandments: respect for life. Jesus makes it a test of observance of the Law. Beyond physical murder, the Bible sees it as a radical injustice against the image of God in every person. For the believer, this word weighs heavily in the moral conscience: it marks the boundary between obedience and rebellion against God.

sens: The act of killing a human being by shedding blood
A criminal act, a violent crime
A murderous intent, a desire to kill
A grave sin, a transgression of God's law
G5408.detail:
1. Murder is the act of intentionally killing someone, often violently. The word directly evokes bloodshed (Hebrews 11:37 speaks of those who were killed by the sword, "murder by the sword"). It is a concrete human crime, like that of Barabbas imprisoned for murder committed during a revolt (Mark 15:7).
2. It is a criminal act that falls under criminal justice: Luke 23:19 shows that one was imprisoned for murder, just as for sedition. Murder was among the serious crimes punished by authorities.
3. Murder also expresses a hostile intention of the heart. Jesus lists it among the evil thoughts and desires that spring from the human heart (Matthew 15:19, Mark 7:21) — it is a deadly malice, a desire to destroy others.
4. From a biblical perspective, it is a major sin: Paul lists it among the works of the flesh opposed to the Spirit (Romans 1:29, Galatians 5:21), and Revelation counts it among the crimes for which men refuse to repent (Revelation 9:21).
G5408.origine: The Greek word *phonos* (φόνος) comes from a root meaning "to kill" or "to strike." It is related to other Greek terms expressing murderous violence. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew *dam* (blood) or expressions denoting voluntary homicide. The underlying image is that of bloodshed — the visible and definitive sign of murder.
G5408.emploi: The word appears about 10 times in the New Testament. It first appears in Matthew and Mark, where Jesus lists the sins that defile the human heart (Matthew 15:19, Mark 7:21): murder comes from within a man as an expression of his sinful nature. Luke uses it in the political context of Barabbas and Pilate (Luke 23:19, 25): concrete murders justifying imprisonment. Saul in Acts 9:1 "was breathing" murder against the disciples — a fierce intention. Paul in Romans 1:29 ranks murder among the moral vices that God judges. The Epistle to the Hebrews (11:37) mentions saints "put to death by the sword" — murder inflicted on the faithful. Revelation (9:21) emphasizes that men refuse to repent of their murders: the term then designates both the criminal act and the spiritual refusal to amend.
G5408.portee: Murder is presented in the Bible not only as a criminal offense but as the ultimate expression of hatred and the sin of the human heart. By naming it, Jesus and the apostles reveal that the true source of evil is not only the external act but the inner malice. For the believer, this invites examination not only of actions but of intentions toward others: unjust anger, vengeance, the desire to harm, are the roots of murder. It is a call to the conversion of the heart.

sens: To habitually wear, to have on oneself clothing or adornments
To carry a weapon, equipment, a symbol of authority
To have on oneself, to visibly display
To be clothed with, to be endowed with a nature or quality
G5409.detail:
1. To wear clothing or adornments habitually and characteristically: it is what one regularly wears, what is typical of oneself. In Matthew 11:8, the word describes those who wear fine clothing, that is, who don them as a sign of wealth and social status.
2. To carry a weapon or a symbol of authority: in Romans 13:4, the magistrate bears the sword, not just occasionally, but constantly, as a badge of his mission as God's avenger — it is what equips him for his role.
3. To visibly display on oneself: in John 19:5, Jesus bears the crown of thorns and the purple robe, objects that cover him and identify him at the moment of his judgment and death. It is a visible and permanent presence during that time.
4. To be clothed with a nature or moral and spiritual quality: in 1 Corinthians 15:49, bearing the image of the earthly then of the heavenly means being deeply marked by this nature, embodying it in one's entire being.
G5409.origine: The word comes from the simple verb φέρω (to bear, to bring) to which a prefix is added indicating repetition or habit. This is why φορέω does not denote an occasional bearing, but a habitual and characteristic bearing, something that one constantly has on oneself. The root refers to the idea of supporting, maintaining, having with oneself durably.
G5409.emploi: The verb φορέω appears five times in the New Testament, always to express a habitual action or a stable state. In Matthew 11:8 and James 2:3, it concerns clothing that marks social status: one wears the magnificent garment or the precious garment, a sign of wealth and position. In John 19:5, it describes Jesus covered with the insignia of mockery (crown and robe), a strong image of the moment of his Passion. In Romans 13:4, the magistrate's sword is not just a tool he uses, but the equipment that defines him in his function: he bears it constantly. Finally, in 1 Corinthians 15:49, the verb is used figuratively to express the incarnation of a spiritual nature: we will bear the image of the heavenly, meaning we will be completely marked and transformed by it.
G5409.portee: This word helps the reader grasp that the Bible speaks not of passing gestures, but of lasting and identifying characters. To wear a garment is what defines me socially; to carry a weapon is what equips me for my mission; to bear a nature is what transforms me deeply. This illuminates how the Christian life is not a series of isolated acts, but a stable state: we become bearers of the new life in Christ, marked even in our being by his resurrection.

sens: Public market and administrative center of a Roman city
Place of gathering and commerce
G5410.detail:
1. In Roman cities, the Forum is equivalent to the public square: it is a large space where the market was held, where magistrates administered justice, and where political and social life took place. The word comes from Latin and refers to a typically Roman institution. In Acts 28:15, Paul goes to the "Forum of Appius" (Ἀππίου Φόρον), an important stopping point on the Appian Way, about 65 km from Rome: it is a natural meeting point where Christians from Rome could wait for and welcome the apostle.
2. The Forum is the living heart of a city: a place of commerce, meetings, political and religious exchanges. This open space symbolizes Roman collective life, which is quite different from that of the Jews. This unique biblical usage shows how the Greek of the New Testament accommodates the realities of the contemporary Roman world to situate events in their concrete framework.
G5410.origine: The word φόρον is a direct borrowing from the Latin forum, which designates the central public space of each Roman city. The authors of the New Testament, writing in Greek but within a Roman empire, borrow this word to name a Roman urban reality for which the Greeks had no direct equivalent — ancient Greece had the agora (ἀγορά), but the Roman forum was a specific institution. This borrowing reflects the direct contact between Greek culture and Roman domination in the first century.
G5410.emploi: The word φόρον appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:15, in the narrative of Paul's journey to Rome. Paul, a prisoner traveling by land after his shipwreck, is welcomed at the Forum of Appius by Christian brothers who came from Rome to meet him. This place is an important stop on the Via Appia, the main road connecting Rome to the southern ports, about 65 km from the capital. Luke mentions this Forum to geographically and socially situate a key moment in Paul's missionary journey: it is a nodal point in the Roman road network where the already established Roman Church can meet the imprisoned apostle.
G5410.portee: This simple yet precise word reminds us that the early Church was unfolding not on the margins, but within the structures and real places of the Roman world: roads, cities, public squares. The mention of the Forum of Appius emphasizes how God guided Paul through the Roman empire, and how Christian brothers risked welcoming a prisoner awaiting trial. It is a vivid detail that anchors the Gospel in concrete history.

sens: Tax paid by a people subjected to their ruler
Dues required from a nation defeated by its conqueror
What is owed to authority in exchange for peace and order
G5411.detail:
1. The tribute is the tax paid by a people subjected to their ruler or conqueror. When the Jews ask Jesus if it is lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, they are questioning the obligation to the Roman power that occupies their land (Luke 20:22). It is a forced contribution, a recognition of political domination.
2. It is also the dues demanded from a defeated nation to obtain peace and order. The accusation against Jesus mentions that he would have prevented people from paying tribute to Caesar (Luke 23:2): for the occupier, it is a regular income, a right of the one who holds power.
3. More broadly, it is what is owed to the established authority. Paul uses it in Romans 13:6-7 when he explains that Christians must pay their taxes: the tribute is presented as a just debt to those who govern.
G5411.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to bear" (φέρω). The tribute is literally what one bears, what one regularly brings as an obligation. In Hebrew, it corresponds to the word מַס (mas), which designates the tax or compulsory labor imposed by a king. It is a word of political domination and submission.
G5411.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, concentrated in two key passages: the questions to Jesus about Caesar (Luke 20:22 and 23:2) and Paul's teaching on obedience to authorities (Romans 13:6-7). Luke sometimes refers to it as "tribute" (imposed on Jerusalem by Rome), and sometimes as "revolt tribute" (in 23:2, since the accusation against Jesus was that he incited people to refuse the tribute). Paul prefers the term "tax" to discuss it in a context of Christian ethics, but it refers to the same obligation.
G5411.portee: This word highlights a central tension: should the Christian obey an unbelieving power? Luke poses the question frankly; Paul answers by affirming that paying taxes is a duty of conscience toward the established order. The tribute reminds that disciples live in a political world, and that submission to civil authorities is compatible with faith in Jesus.

sens: To load a burden, a weight on someone or something
Figuratively: to impose a moral or spiritual burden on someone
To be burdened, to be overloaded (passive sense)
G5412.detail:
1. The literal sense: to load someone with a physical weight, a material burden. This is the basic meaning of the verb. Jesus reproaches the teachers of the law for loading people (Luke 11:46), that is, imposing obligations that are difficult to bear.
2. In a figurative sense: to impose a moral, spiritual, or emotional weight on someone — precepts, rules, guilt. The Pharisees "load" their disciples with numerous and rigorous laws, weighing down their conscience.
3. To be loaded, burdened, overloaded: this is the passive sense of the verb. In Matthew 11:28, Jesus invites "all you who are weary and burdened" — that is, crushed under the weight of religious obligations and life — to come to him for rest.
G5412.origine: The verb φορτίζω comes from the noun φόρτος (phortus), which means "load," "burden," "cargo." It is a word related to transport: one loads a ship, one loads a beast of burden. The Hebrew word שָׁחַד (shakhad, "to corrupt" or "to be corrupted") in Ezekiel 16:33 shows how a burden can symbolize an obligation or seduction.
G5412.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament. In Luke 11:46, Jesus uses it in the active form to denounce the teachers of the law who overload the people with legal prescriptions without helping them bear them. In Matthew 11:28, he uses the passive form to invite those who are "burdened" — overwhelmed — to come seek rest with him. In this latter context, "burdened" contrasts with "rest" (anapaúsis): it is the image of the burden that crushes spiritual life.
G5412.portee: This word reveals the heart of Jesus' critique of religious legalism: imposing burdens without offering relief is a spiritual violence. For the Christian, this term reminds that Jesus does not load but unloads, that he removes the crushing weight of guilt and works. It is an invitation to true freedom and rest.

sens: Material load, cargo transported by a ship or an animal
Obligation, commandment, or responsibility imposed on someone
Moral or spiritual weight that weighs on the conscience or soul
G5413.detail:
1. The burden is primarily a concrete load: it is what is loaded onto a ship, like the cargo of a boat (Acts 27:10 refers to the cargo of the ship on which Paul is traveling to Rome). It is the image of the weight placed on the shoulders or that one carries.

2. In terms of religious duties, a burden is an obligation, a law, or a commandment imposed on someone. The teachers of the law, Jesus says, load people with "heavy burdens" (Matthew 23:4) — the traditions and rules they add to the Law, without caring whether they can be borne.

3. Spiritually, it is the inner weight that each person carries: their own responsibilities, sins, trials. Jesus says that his yoke is easy and his burden is light (Matthew 11:30), promising that following Christ lightens the soul. Each person carries their own burden (Galatians 6:5), their personal responsibility before God.
G5413.origine: The word comes from the Greek φόρος (phoros), which means "to bear," and the diminutive "-ion" makes it a lighter or more limited load. In Hebrew, the corresponding main word is משׂא (massa), the burden or weight that one lifts. The family of the word encompasses terms related to transport and weight: this root is found in other Greek words describing what one carries or imposes.
G5413.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. In Matthew and Luke, it refers to the burdens that the teachers impose on the faithful — stifling legalism and human traditions (Matthew 23:4, Luke 11:46). In Jesus' words, in Matthew 11:30, it is a contrast: the burden he brings is "light," bearing grace and not oppression. In Acts 27:10, the word returns to its concrete meaning: the cargo of the ship. In Galatians 6:5, Paul uses it spiritually: each must bear their own burden, their personal moral responsibility. The meaning always shifts between concrete (material load) and figurative (obligation, moral weight).
G5413.portee: This word helps the Christian understand the difference between the crushing Law wielded by the teachers and the easy yoke of Jesus: faith in Christ does not add weights, it lightens and liberates. It also reminds us that everyone has their personal responsibilities before God (Galatians 6:5), which cannot be left to others, and that we must help each other carry them together (Galatians 6:2). It is a word of freedom and realism: freedom from legalism, realism regarding our duties.

sens: Christian man from Corinth in the first century
G5415.detail: Fortunatus is a Christian from Corinth mentioned briefly in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians. His name, of Latin origin, means "the fortunate" or "the lucky." He is mentioned alongside Stephanas and Achaicus as someone who filled the absence of the church in Corinth before Paul, likely by visiting him and bringing news of the local church (1 Corinthians 16:17).
G5415.origine: The name Fortunatus is of Latin origin and literally means "fortunate" or "lucky," derived from the Latin word "fortuna" (fortune, luck). It is a typical name of the inhabitants of the Roman world, reflecting the Greek and Roman environment of Corinth at the apostolic time.
G5415.emploi: Fortunatus appears twice in Paul's epistles: in 1 Corinthians 16:17, where Paul mentions him alongside Stephanas and Achaicus as someone who visited him and filled the absence of the church in Corinth, and in 1 Corinthians 16:24, where Paul includes him in his final greetings. These brief mentions suggest that Fortunatus was a respected figure in the church of Corinth, active in service and fellowship with the apostle.
G5415.portee: Fortunatus reminds us that the early Church was made up of ordinary people, often converts from the Greco-Roman world, who engaged concretely in service and hospitality towards the apostles. His example shows the importance of practical support and brotherly fellowship in the life of the local church.

sens: instrument made of cords or strips used to strike
punishment, chastisement inflicted by the whip
G5416.detail:
1. The whip is a punishment instrument made of cords or strips attached to a handle: in John 2:15, Jesus makes a whip of cords to drive the merchants out of the temple, thus demonstrating the strength of his action and the seriousness of his authority.
2. The whip more broadly represents punishment or suffering inflicted by violence: it is a tool of discipline and punishment, whether used by a master against slaves or, symbolically, by God against sinners.
G5416.origine: The Greek word φραγέλλιον (phragellion) comes directly from the Latin "flagellum," which means whip. This borrowing shows how Roman life influenced the Greek of the New Testament: the Romans used the whip as a common punishment instrument, especially for slaves and criminals. The word evokes the very concrete image of a tool of chastisement.
G5416.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 2:15. Jesus makes a whip of cords to purify the temple, not to harm people, but to manifest his authority and indignation at the commerce and desecration of the holy place. This spectacular gesture shows that Jesus expresses himself not only through words but also through strong and symbolic actions.
G5416.portee: This passage reveals that Jesus, far from being a passive and solely compassionate figure, acts with authority and courage against what desecrates the temple of God. For the Christian, this teaches that authentic faith may require decisive actions against evil and injustice, and that the house of God deserves to be respected and protected.

sens: To strike someone with an instrument of multiple cords or strips
To inflict particularly painful corporal punishment
G5417.detail:
1. To whip means to strike methodically with an instrument called a flagellum or rod, made of several strips. It is a brutal act that wounds the skin and causes intense suffering. In Matthew 27:26 and Mark 15:15, the Roman soldiers whip Jesus before his crucifixion: it is a preparatory torture meant to weaken the condemned.
2. More broadly, to whip refers to the infliction of particularly violent and humiliating corporal punishment. It is a punishment that Roman law applied to criminals sentenced to death, often before the final execution. The whipping of Jesus thus shows his humiliation and acceptance of suffering.
G5417.origine: The Greek word φραγελλόω (phragelloō) comes from the name φραγέλλιον (phragellion), which designates the whip or rod with multiple strips. This name comes from the Latin "flagellum," borrowed by Greek to describe this typical punishment instrument of Roman justice. It is therefore a word imported through commerce and administration: the Greeks of the New Testament use this term for a Roman instrument.
G5417.emploi: The verb φραγελλόω appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the Passion narratives: Matthew 27:26 and Mark 15:15. These two passages report exactly the same moment: Pilate, the Roman governor, orders that Jesus be whipped before being handed over for crucifixion. It is a legal act of torture in the Roman judicial system, distinct from the final execution. The use of the word remains strictly limited to this dramatic historical event, without metaphor or figurative extension.
G5417.portee: The whipping of Jesus reveals the extent of his sacrifice: he suffers not only death but also prior sufferings that humiliate and cause him pain. By willingly accepting this, he shows his compassion for our sins and the price of our redemption. This brutal detail of the Gospel narrative reminds us that the cross was not only shameful but physically atrocious.

sens: Fence or barrier that encloses an area
Figuratively: that which separates, that which divides
G5418.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a hedge is a fence that surrounds and protects an area — for example, a man's vineyard. In Matthew 21:33 and Mark 12:1, Jesus speaks of a master who plants a vineyard and surrounds it with a hedge to delineate and defend it. It is a physical, concrete barrier made of bushes or intertwined materials.
2. Figuratively, the hedge becomes an image of separation and division between peoples. In Ephesians 2:14, Paul speaks of the "dividing wall," of which the hedge is the symbolic equivalent: it creates distance, rupture, and enmity between two groups. Here, it refers to the spiritual and social barrier between Jews and Gentiles.
G5418.origine: The Greek word φραγμός comes from the verb φράσσω which means "to enclose" or "to barricade." It denotes the action of "fencing in," creating an enclosure. In Hebrew, it corresponds mainly to גָּדֵר (gadêr) and גְּדֵרָה (gedêrâh), terms that describe a wall or a fence. The root evokes the fundamental idea of "delineating" an area, separating the inside from the outside.
G5418.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. Three occurrences are found in the parable of the vineyard (Matthew 21:33, Mark 12:1, Luke 14:23): in the first two, the hedge physically surrounds the vineyard to protect and delineate it; in the third, it refers to property boundaries along the roads, in other words, the borders of lands. A fourth occurrence in Ephesians 2:14 uses the word figuratively: Paul sees it as an image of the separation between Jews and non-Jews, a spiritual barrier that Christ has destroyed. This passage shows how the same word oscillates between concrete and metaphorical meanings.
G5418.portee: The concrete hedge of the parable reminds the believer that God cares for what belongs to Him, delineating and protecting His Church. But the passage in Ephesians goes further: the destruction of this "hedge" of separation announces that Christ has reconciled in Himself what was divided. For the Christian, it is a call to live in unity in Christ beyond any human barrier.

sens: To make known the meaning of something by clearly revealing it
To help understand a word or riddle by clarifying it
G5419.detail:
1. The verb φράζω means to show clearly, to make manifest what was hidden or unclear. It is to explain by revealing the true meaning. In Matthew 15:15, the disciples ask Jesus: "Explain this parable to us" — they want Jesus to show them the hidden meaning of the words He has just spoken.
2. By extension, it means to make heard, interpret, declare the meaning of a riddle or obscure word. The word evokes the action of making transparent what was opaque, moving from ignorance to clear understanding.
G5419.origine: The word φράζω comes from a root that fundamentally means "to show," "to make see." In Hebrew, the Greek Pentateuch translated forms of the verb בִּין ("to understand"), יָרָה ("to teach"), and חָוָה ("to make known"). It is a term that emphasizes the transition from darkness to light, from the incomprehensible to the comprehensible.
G5419.emploi: This verb appears rarely in the New Testament. The main usage is in Matthew 15:15, where the disciples ask Jesus to explain the parable of the unclean foods. Matthew 13:36 also contains a similar request: the disciples plead with Jesus to explain (using the related verb διασάφησον) the parable of the weeds. These two occurrences show that the verb is mainly used in a pedagogical context: a teacher who dispels confusion by making clear what was wrapped in an image or parable.
G5419.portee: This word reminds us that following Jesus does not mean remaining in confusion: He invites us to ask for explanations about His words, just as the disciples did. It is an invitation to spiritual clarity, a refusal to remain in darkness, and the believer's right to seek to understand God's teaching.

sens: To physically close, block the passage
To prevent from speaking, silence
To stop, interrupt something
G5420.detail:
1. In the literal sense, to close means to block access or seal an opening: this is what one does with a door, a lion's mouth. The heroes of faith "stopped the mouths of lions" (Hebrews 11:33), meaning that by the power of God, they took away the lions' ability to bite.
2. Metaphorically, to close a mouth means to prevent someone from speaking, to silence them. In Romans 3:19, "every mouth" must be "closed" before God — no one will have any excuse or argument to give in the face of divine judgment.
3. More broadly, to close means to stop or interrupt: one can take away from someone a "subject of glory" (2 Corinthians 11:10), meaning to remove their ability to boast.
G5420.origine: The word comes from a root that refers to the idea of closing, blocking. In ancient Greek, it initially designated the act of building a fence or wall. The preposition that composes it suggests the idea of completely locking. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it often renders the Hebrew סָכַךְ (to cover, protect, close) or שׂוּךְ (to surround).
G5420.emploi: The verb "to close" appears three times in the New Testament in French translation. In Hebrews 11:33, it describes the miraculous action of closing the mouths of lions. In Romans 3:19, Paul uses it metaphorically: the mouths must be closed, meaning that no one can contest the divine verdict of universal guilt. In 2 Corinthians 11:10, it means rather to take away, to remove: to take away someone's subject of pride. The word thus shifts between the physical image of locking and the abstract idea of deprivation or imposed silence.
G5420.portee: This word reminds us of God's absolute sovereignty: He can close the mouths of predators to protect His own, and He also closes the mouths of all humanity in the face of His judgment. No excuse holds before Him. It is a word of comfort for believers in danger, and a word of warning for everyone: there is no escape from divine judgment.

sens: A hole dug in the ground to access water
A deep passage leading to underground depths or to the abyss
G5421.detail:
1. A well is a hole dug vertically in the ground to draw water. It is a common installation in the ancient Near East, essential for life. Jesus refers to it in Luke 14:5 as an example of urgency that takes precedence over Sabbath rest: one saves an animal that has fallen into a well without waiting until the next day. The Samaritan woman reminds Jesus of Jacob's deep well in John 4:11-12, a precious heritage that the ancestors dug and used — a place of daily life and family memory.
2. By extension, the well denotes an entrance to hidden or dark depths. In Revelation 9:1-2, it becomes the "bottomless pit": not an ordinary well, but the key to access the abyss, that chasm of evil forces imprisoned beneath the earth. When the angel opens it, a thick smoke emerges that darkens the sky — the cosmic well revealed as a passage to a formidable chaos.
G5421.origine: The Greek word φρέαρ almost always translates the Hebrew בְּאֵר (be'er), which literally means "digging" or "excavation." The root evokes the action of digging, forcing a passage into the earth. It is a familiar word in the Semitic world, where underground water is a vital treasure. In Revelation, the same word takes on a symbolic charge: the concrete well becomes a cosmic door.
G5421.emploi: The word appears 5 times in Luke and John, in very different contexts. Luke 14:5 uses it in a mundane way: an ordinary well where an animal falls on the Sabbath. John 4:11-12 places it in the dialogue with the Samaritan woman, where Jacob's well is an ancestral asset, a transmitted property, a source of physical living water — but where Jesus speaks of it enigmatically as a figure of the water He gives. In Revelation 9:1-2, the language changes: the well is no longer earthly; it is a cosmic well, a key that opens the abyss. It is the same concrete word applied to a spiritual and eschatological reality, showing how Revelation integrates traditional biblical imagery to speak of the hidden mysteries of God.
G5421.portee: The well reminds us that water, a vital good, is hidden and requires work to be reached. Jesus offers water that springs forth as an eternal source, without effort or equipment. For the reader, it is an invitation to understand that true life comes from God alone — living water that the world, with all its traditional wells, cannot provide. Revelation adds: behind the visible world, a formidable depth remains sealed by God; and in sacred history, this seal can be opened. It is an invitation to vigilance and trust.

sens: To deceive oneself by forming a false opinion of one's own merit or abilities
To be fooled by one's own thoughts or illusions
G5422.detail:
1. To deceive means here to mislead one's own mind: it is to lie to oneself about what one truly is. In Galatians 6:3, the one who thinks he is something important when he is nothing commits this serious error — he deceives himself, a victim of his own distorted judgment. The image is that of an inner deception: one deceives oneself when one believes one's own lies or flattering illusions.
2. The word thus designates a form of personal disappointment, often involuntary: one does not deceive someone else, but oneself. It is to be seduced by false thoughts about one's worth, knowledge, or power, which prevents one from seeing the truth.
G5422.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: "phren" (the mind, heart, thought) and "apataō" (to deceive, disappoint). Literally, it means "to deceive the mind" or "to deceive the heart." This composition clearly shows the meaning: the deception targets the very center of the person, their judgment and conscience. The word specifically denotes this self-illusion where one becomes the victim of one's own distorted thoughts.
G5422.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 6:3. Paul uses it to warn those who might have an overly high opinion of themselves. He denounces this illusion of superiority — one deceives oneself when one believes oneself to be something when one is nothing in the eyes of God. It is a serious form of spiritual pride: not only does one deceive oneself, but one deceives oneself about the most important thing, one's relationship with God and one's true spiritual worth.
G5422.portee: This word invites the reader to honesty with oneself: it reminds us that pride begins with an inner deception, with a distorted view of who we really are. Before God, one cannot lie to oneself for long without consequences. The passage in Galatians 6:3 calls for true humility, based on a correct perception of our condition: we are nothing without the grace of God, and to deceive ourselves on this point is to distance ourselves from the truth.

sens: One who deceives others by leading them into error or misdirection
One who deceives oneself about one's own nature or actions
G5423.detail:
1. A deceiver is a person who deceives others — they mislead, misdirect, and lead others to believe or do what is false or contrary to the truth. It is an intentional deceiver who acts to mislead others. In Titus 1:10, Paul designates by this word the troublemakers who speak vainly and seek to seduce Christians with false doctrines.
2. The word can also refer to one who deceives oneself — that is, who lies to oneself about one's own nature or actions. This person gives themselves a false opinion of themselves and lives in illusion regarding who they really are.
G5423.origine: The word comes from the root "φρήν" (mind, heart, seat of thought) and "ἀπάτη" (deception, illusion). It literally designates one who deceives the mind — who misleads judgment and reason. The same root "ἀπάτη" (deception) appears in other New Testament terms to describe misdirection and lies.
G5423.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 1:10, where Paul warns Titus about false teachers who threaten the Church. Paul characterizes them as "rebels," "vain talkers," and "deceivers" — in other words, men who sow confusion and doctrinal error, particularly among converted Judeans. It is a pejorative term, designating a category of ecclesiastical troublemakers.
G5423.portee: This word highlights the spiritual danger posed by those who deceive others through lies and doctrinal error. It invites the Christian to remain vigilant, not to be seduced, and to test the words taught to them in the light of the Word of God. It is a call to caution and discernment in the face of false teachers.

sens: The part of the body associated with thought and emotions, notably the heart and diaphragm
The mind, the ability to think and reflect
The intention, the inner disposition of a person
The discernment, the ability to judge and evaluate things
G5424.detail:
1. In the physical sense, the word primarily refers to the organs of the body related to thought — the heart, the diaphragm — seen as the seat of spiritual and mental life. The ancient Greeks viewed these parts as the center of intelligence and emotions, similar to how we say "having a beating heart" when we are moved.

2. By extension, φρήν means the mind itself, the capacity to think and reason. It is living intelligence, reflection in action, the inner life of a person.

3. The word also denotes the intention or disposition of the heart — what truly resides within us, beyond appearances. In 1 Corinthians 14:20, Paul urges Christians to "not be children in regard to judgment," meaning: do not remain childish in your way of thinking and judging.

4. Finally, it expresses discernment, the ability to evaluate, to discern, to judge what is right or wrong. It is the mature exercise of reason and conscience.
G5424.origine: The Greek word φρήν comes from an ancient root meaning "to separate" or "to divide." In ancient Greek thought, it originally referred to the diaphragm or the region of the heart, conceived as the seat of feelings and thought. It is used in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) primarily to render the Hebrew לֵב (leb), which means heart and represents the center of inner life, will, and judgment. This connection between the physical organ and mental capacity reflects an ancient view of the body and spirit as intimately linked.
G5424.emploi: The word φρήν appears very rarely in the New Testament — a single certain occurrence in 1 Corinthians 14:20. Paul uses it to call Christians to spiritual maturity: "do not be children in regard to judgment." He invites them to move beyond mental and moral immaturity, to cultivate adult and discerning thought. In ancient Greece, the word was common in classical texts (Homer, Greek tragedies, Plato) to refer to both the physical heart and the mind and reason. In the Septuagint, it regularly translates the Hebrew "heart," emphasizing the dimension of judgment and reflection.
G5424.portee: This word reminds the believer that Christian maturity involves the formation of the mind. Paul urges us not to remain childish in our judgment, but to cultivate right, thoughtful, and wise thinking. It is a call to exercise discernment, to develop the ability to evaluate what is good, to grow in spiritual intelligence. For the Christian, this means: deepening one's understanding of the faith, not being tossed about by trends or emotions, but acquiring wisdom in decisions and relationships.

sens: To have goosebumps, to shiver
To tremble in fear, to be seized with dread
To express through a shudder a visceral reaction of horror or fear
G5425.detail:
1. The word first evokes an immediate physical reaction of the body: the skin bristles, one shivers, as when cold or when a repulsion seizes us. It is an involuntary contraction that manifests intense emotion.

2. To tremble in fear or dread: it is to experience a fear so deep that it shakes the entire body. In James 2:19, demons "tremble" at the thought of God — not simply a trivial fear, but a terror that grips them at their very core, for they know who God is and the judgment that awaits them.

3. This trembling is not affectation: it is a reaction of the flesh and heart in the face of something frightening or incomprehensible, a kind of shudder that reveals the truth of what one feels deep within.
G5425.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that depicts a wavering movement, shivering, or bristling. It appears in ancient Greek with variations (Attic -ττω instead of -σσ-). It is found in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) notably in Job 4:15, describing a physical reaction of terror. The family of the word revolves around the idea of contraction, spasmodic movement of the body in response to strong emotion.
G5425.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 2:19. The apostle uses it in an argument against a dead and purely intellectual faith: "You believe that there is one God, you do well; the demons believe it too, and they tremble." The context is striking: true faith is not reduced to a mental or doctrinal adherence. The demons, on the other hand, believe in the existence of God and react with their whole being — they tremble, seized with fear before the one they know is above them. This trembling of the demons contrasts with the inertia of the believer who merely claims to believe without ever acting accordingly.
G5425.portee: This verse reminds us that true faith is not just about intellectually accepting truths about God, but being transformed by that knowledge. Even demons "know" — and this knowledge frightens them. It shakes them. For the Christian, the question is: does my faith in God shake me enough to change my life? Or am I paralyzed like the believer in James who believes but does not act?

sens: to have understanding, to comprehend
to have a thought, a conviction about something
to hold a certain opinion, to form a judgment
to have something in mind, to be attached to it
to share the same mindset, to be of the same sentiment
G5426.detail:
1. To have understanding means to possess the ability to comprehend and reason. This is the simplest meaning of the verb, which designates the mental activity itself (1 Corinthians 13:11: "I thought like a child").

2. To have a thought or a conviction about something means to form an opinion, a judgment. Paul writes to the Romans that one must "think" according to what God requires, not according to pride (Romans 12:3: "Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but think of yourself with sober judgment").

3. To hold a certain opinion means to adopt a particular mental position. When Jesus rebukes Peter by saying, "You are not mindful of the things of God, but the things of men" (Matthew 16:23), he indicates the orientation of his conviction.

4. To have something in mind, to be attached to it: the verb describes what occupies our mind and heart. "Those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit set their minds on the things of the Spirit" (Romans 8:5) — here, "to think" means to direct one's desire and attention.

5. To share the same mindset expresses unity of spirit among believers. "Be of the same mind toward one another" (Romans 12:16) invites us to "think" together, to form a common conviction.
G5426.origine: The word comes from φρήν (phrên), which literally designates the diaphragm, the seat of intelligence and feelings in ancient Greek thought. This word has given rise to a rich family: φρόνιμος (prudent, wise), φρονίμως (wisely), and also the compounds περι-φρονέω (to have a high opinion of oneself), ὑπερ-φρονέω (to be presumptuous). In Hebrew, it primarily translates חָכַם (to be wise), שָׂכַל (to understand, to be intelligent), and בִּין (to discern).
G5426.emploi: The verb φρονέω appears 22 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles (Romans, 1-2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, Colossians). Paul uses it in three main contexts: first, to express spiritual orientation (to fear God or to yield to the desires of the flesh), then to evoke the unity of soul among believers ("to think the same thing"), and finally to describe a personal opinion or judgment one has about someone. In Matthew 16:23 and Mark 8:33, Jesus uses it to denounce Peter's carnal mentality that opposes the Father's plan. The word thus oscillates between the simple activity of thinking and a deep attachment to certain values.
G5426.portee: This verb calls the believer to examine what reigns in their heart and mind. "Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth" (Colossians 3:2) invites a constant renewal of one's mindset. Cultivating true unity with other Christians requires "thinking the same thing" (Philippians 2:2, 2:5), not through conformity, but through a common attachment to Christ. This word shows that true faith is not a mere verbal profession, but a transformation of heart and mind, a redirection of our thoughts toward what pleases God.

sens: What occupies and directs the mind, the orientation of thought
The sum of thoughts and desires that govern a person
What the heart tends toward
The deep moral and spiritual attitude
G5427.detail:
1. The word designates what fills the mind, what directs it. It is the content of thought — not an isolated idea, but the general direction toward which thought turns. In Romans 8:6-7, Paul uses it to designate the orientation of our entire mental and emotional life: "the mind of the flesh" is what one thinks and aspires to when living according to fleshly impulses, while "the mind of the Spirit" is what one aspires to when led by the Spirit of God.
2. More broadly, it is the sum of thoughts, desires, and attitudes that govern a person — their overall mentality. A person can have the mind of the flesh (self-centered, focused on pleasures, power) or the mind of the Spirit (turned toward God, obedient, loving). These two minds are in constant conflict: one leads to death, the other to life and peace.
3. It is also what characterizes the Spirit itself: in Romans 8:27, Paul speaks of "the mind of the Spirit" — what he intercedes for the saints according to the heart of God.
G5427.origine: The word comes from the verb phronéō (φρονέω), which means "to think, to have an opinion, to be of a certain mind." It designates the product of this mental activity: what results from thinking, that is, the enduring orientation of thought, the state of mind. It is less a fleeting thought than a mentality, a stable inner disposition. The word carries the idea of a thought that takes root, which directs the whole person.
G5427.emploi: Paul uses this word three times, exclusively in Romans 8:6-7 and 8:27, in a fundamental passage about life according to the Spirit. He contrasts the mind of the flesh (which is enmity against God and cannot submit to His law) with the mind of the Spirit (which brings life and peace). These minds are not fleeting feelings, but deep orientations: they define the path each person takes. The mind of the flesh produces death; the mind of the Spirit, interceding according to God's will, produces life.
G5427.portee: This word reminds us that what truly governs us is not isolated actions, but the overall orientation of our mind. Are we turned toward our own desires and independence (mind of the flesh), or toward God and His Spirit (mind of the Spirit)? This biblical distinction invites the Christian to examine what truly fills their heart and directs their existence, and to ask the Holy Spirit to transform their mentality.

sens: Ability to discern good from evil and to act with prudence
Aptitude to understand what is appropriate in every circumstance
Wise understanding of divine and spiritual matters
G5428.detail:
1. Practical wisdom is the ability to judge well and to act wisely in concrete life. It is not mere theoretical knowledge, but prudence that guides decisions. In Luke 1:17, the forerunner of the Lord will walk with this practical wisdom to turn hearts toward good.

2. It is also the aptitude to understand what is right and fitting in every situation, to discern true from false. In Ephesians 1:8, God pours out this practical understanding upon us, as a gift that helps us navigate spiritual matters with discernment.

3. This wisdom carries a moral dimension: it directs not only thought but also conduct. It brings closer to the righteous and the straight paths, producing wisdom in those who receive it.
G5428.origine: The word comes from the verb "to think, to be prudent" and designates the fruit of thoughtful consideration. It has the root of reflection and balanced judgment. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew terms for "discernment" and "understanding" — these terms that describe the wisdom of one who knows God and knows how to conduct themselves according to His will. It is a wisdom oriented toward right action, not mere speculation.
G5428.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 1:17, it characterizes the ministry of the Forerunner: he will receive the spirit of Elijah and walk in practical wisdom capable of converting rebellious hearts. In Ephesians 1:8, it is presented as a divine gift, a grace that God abundantly gives us so that we may understand and do His will. In both cases, it is a wisdom that has concrete and transformative effects.
G5428.portee: For the Christian, this practical wisdom is a gift that God grants to discern His will and live wisely. It is not a virtue acquired solely by effort, but a grace that God pours out on those who ask for it. It enables us to conduct ourselves prudently in a world that often does not understand God's ways, and it helps to bring others back to the truth.

sens: Who acts with common sense and practical discernment
Who is wise in managing affairs and resources
Who makes thoughtful and judicious decisions
Who opposes carelessness or lack of foresight
Wise in one's own opinion, overly confident in one's reasoning
G5429.detail:
1. The word describes one who acts with common sense in concrete life. It is not a theoretical wisdom, but the ability to make the right choices: Jesus compares the one who hears his words and puts them into practice to a wise man who builds his house on the rock (Matthew 7:24), for he builds on a solid and lasting foundation.

2. Prudence is especially seen in the management of affairs and resources. The wise servant whom his master appoints over his household to give them their food at the proper time (Matthew 24:45) knows how to administer, foresee, and act wisely. The wise virgins who took oil in reserve (Matthew 25:4) demonstrate this concrete foresight.

3. It is the opposite of folly and carelessness. Paul writes that the children of this age are more prudent toward their peers than the children of light (Luke 16:8): the people of the world know how to calculate and plan for their temporal interests, but believers often lack this same sagacity in spiritual life.

4. Prudence includes humility and self-doubt. Jesus warns his disciples to be wise as serpents but innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16): to be prudent is to recognize dangers. Not being wise in one's own eyes (Romans 12:16) means rejecting this false wisdom where everyone believes they are right and considers themselves more discerning than they are.
G5429.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb φρονέω ("to think, to have feelings"), which denotes the activity of the mind and judgment. φρόνιμος thus describes one whose thinking functions well, who knows how to reflect correctly. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word primarily translates בִּין ("to discern, to understand") and חָכָם ("to be wise"), showing that biblical wisdom is primarily a matter of practical discernment: seeing rightly and acting accordingly.
G5429.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in the Gospel of Matthew and in Paul's epistles. Matthew uses it to describe those who build their lives on a solid foundation (7:24), the faithful servants (24:45), and the prudent virgins (25:2-9). Paul reserves it more for critique: he warns against those who think they are wise in their own eyes (Romans 11:25; 12:16), emphasizing that true prudence requires a certain humility. In Luke 16:8, Jesus ironically notes that the people of the world are sometimes more prudent in their affairs than the disciples are in the things of the Kingdom. The word clearly opposes folly (μωρός) and carelessness (ἄφρων).
G5429.portee: For the Christian, prudence is not cunning or distrust, but a fruit of biblical wisdom: knowing how to discern, foresee, and act with common sense and humility. Jesus does not call us to be naive, but vigilant and thoughtful. Prudence also reminds us that true wisdom begins with the awareness of our limits: not being wise in our own eyes means recognizing that we need God's guidance to discern what is right and useful.

sens: With common sense and sagacity
With prudence and judicious calculation
With practical intelligence regarding realities
G5430.detail:
1. The word primarily means "with common sense" or "with sagacity" — it is acting while fully understanding the situation and its stakes. In the parable of Luke 16:8, the master praises the dishonest steward for having acted prudently: the man used his intelligence to secure his future when he discovered he was going to lose his position, by reducing the debts of the debtors to create obligations for himself.

2. It is also "with practical prudence" — not necessarily a moral prudence, but an execution prudence, which knows how to weigh risks and benefits. The steward acted quickly, discreetly, understanding how the business world operates.

3. The adverb finally suggests "with intelligence of the real": a certain finesse in understanding human relationships and the interests at stake. Jesus does not praise dishonesty, but he emphasizes that this man at least showed more ingenuity and determination than the children of light, who often lack this quick-wittedness in service of their faith.
G5430.origine: The word comes from the root meaning "to think," "to have common sense" (the same family as "phronesis," practical sagacity). It denotes the action of one who thinks rightly and sees clearly — not abstract moral wisdom, but the intelligence that makes informed and realistic choices in light of circumstances.
G5430.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:8, in the parable of the dishonest steward. Jesus recounts how a dishonest servant, discovering he was about to be dismissed, acted prudently — that is, with quick and wise calculation — to improve his situation before losing his job. The context shows that Jesus does not justify his dishonesty, but notes that he at least acted with a certain intelligence, more than often the disciples of the Kingdom do.
G5430.portee: This word invites the reader to a healthy form of vigilance: to act with practical intelligence, to see clearly in the real situations of the world, and even to learn from those who do not seek God how to use sagacity and promptness. Jesus calls his disciples to be at least as wise as the children of this age in their service of the Kingdom — not to deceive, but to discern and act effectively.

sens: To give attention to something, to take care of it
To focus on a task, to strive to accomplish it
To be concerned, worried
G5431.detail:
1. To apply oneself means to direct one's attention toward something with intention and responsibility. It is the thought that fixes on a specific goal. In Titus 3:8, Paul urges Titus to ensure that believers "apply themselves to good works": it is about deliberately paying attention to the good to be done, not neglecting it.
2. This term evokes the conscious and sustained effort to accomplish a task. It is not a passive action, but an active engagement of will and mind. The idea is one of vigilant care, of intentional concern: one must truly "aim" for the good work and dedicate oneself to it.
3. The word can also express worry, concern, or even anxiety regarding something that requires our reflection. It is to be thoughtful, attentive to what concerns us.
G5431.origine: The Greek word φροντίζω comes from the root φροντίς (phrontis), which means "thought" or "concern." It is a verb that expresses the action of thinking, reflecting, and mentally occupying oneself with something. In classical Greek, it is often used without a direct object or with an accusative. The word translates the Hebrew דָּאַג (dâag, "to be anxious") and חָשַׁב (châshab, "to think"), showing that in the ancient Septuagint it conveyed the idea of attentive reflection and concern.
G5431.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 3:8. Paul urges his disciple to strongly affirm the truth of the Gospel "so that those who have believed in God may apply themselves to good works." Here, the emphasis is on the practical will of the believer: to apply oneself to the good work is not only to do it, but to dedicate attention, care, and effort to it. It is a call to active responsibility, to ethical vigilance. The verb implies that good works do not come naturally: they require that one "thinks about it," that one "aims" for it deliberately.
G5431.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds us that the Christian life is not a passive drift. Following Jesus and doing good requires intention, care, and conscious application. It is not enough to want to do well out of sentiment; one must actively direct one's mind and will toward it. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and deliberate engagement in obedience.

sens: Place under surveillance or in safety, protect by active guarding
Maintain in detention or under strict control
Watch over, preserve or protect by an inner or divine force
G5432.detail:
1. To keep primarily means to place something or someone under the protection of an armed guard. It involves actively watching to prevent someone from seizing the thing or person. In 2 Corinthians 11:32, the governor has the gates of Damascus guarded by soldiers to stop Paul.
2. To keep can also mean to hold captive, to maintain under strict control, as one keeps a prisoner. In Galatians 3:23, the Law 'keeps' believers before the arrival of faith, meaning it holds them under its authority, enclosing them as if under close surveillance.
3. Keeping takes on a more spiritual and inner meaning: watching over the heart and mind, preserving from all evil. In Philippians 4:7, the peace of God 'will keep' our hearts and minds — not by external force, but by an intimate divine protection. In 1 Peter 1:5, we are 'kept' by the power of God for salvation.
G5432.origine: The word comes from the Greek phroura, which designates a fortress or a guard post. Phroureō literally means 'to function as a guard' or 'to be on duty.' This military image of guarding has been spiritually enriched in the New Testament to express the divine protection of the believer.
G5432.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament. Three times, it expresses protection or preservation: keeping a city (2 Corinthians 11:32), keeping the heart and mind of the believer (Philippians 4:7), keeping for salvation (1 Peter 1:5). Once, it has a negative nuance: the Law keeps believers, meaning it holds or confines them (Galatians 3:23). In all cases, the idea of a power that watches over, controls, and preserves remains central.
G5432.portee: This word reveals two essential truths to the Christian. First, it reminds us that our protection comes from God alone — not from our own strength or human precautions. Second, it shows that this protection is not a hindrance, but a grace: the believer is not 'confined' by the Law as before, but 'kept' by faith and divine peace that preserve his heart.

sens: Literally refers to a horse that neighs, stirs, and makes noise
Figuratively: to stir with insolence, to make loud and vain noise
G5433.detail:
1. The word paints the concrete image of a horse that neighs, prances, and thrashes about, creating noise and movement. It is the image of raw and disorderly agitation.
2. Used figuratively, it describes men who stir, make a racket and tumult in a haughty and sterile manner. In Acts 4:25, Psalm 2 speaks of the nations and peoples who 'make a tumult' against the Lord: these are the powerful of the earth who stir with arrogance, plotting in vain, creating noise and agitation without foundation.
G5433.origine: The Greek verb φρυάσσομαι originally comes from the world of horses: it designates the neighing and thrashing of a horse, its noisy agitation. This verb has transferred to the haughty agitation of men, their insolent tumult. The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew word רָגַשׁ (ragash) in Psalm 2:1, which means 'to stir, to cover with noise,' the image remaining that of a crowd stirring with a crash.
G5433.emploi: The verb appears only once in Acts 4:25, where Peter and John, released after their imprisonment, pray while quoting Psalm 2. They apply the word to the Sanhedrin and the authorities of Jerusalem who have just questioned them: these religious leaders make a tumult, stir and plot against Jesus, the Messiah, but their agitation is only sterile noise in the face of God's designs. The word evokes the futile insolence of human power that opposes God.
G5433.portee: This word reminds the believer that all human agitation against God and His Messiah, however loud and threatening it may seem, is only vain tumult. Like the horse that stirs without profit, the powerful of this world who rise against Christ make only noise — God remains master of history and accomplishes His counsel unhindered.

sens: Small dry and brittle wood, dead or broken branch
A collection of small woods, twigs, and brushwood
That which is arid, dried out by the sun
G5434.detail:
1. The word first designates a piece of dead wood, a dry and brittle twig — the opposite of green and living wood. In Acts 28:3, Paul gathers dry branches to make a fire on the island of Malta, showing that it is easy to ignite fuel.

2. In the plural (as is the case in the Greek text of Acts 28:3), the word designates a pile of small woods, brushwood, and twigs piled together. The fire quickly catches in this dry mess.

3. The underlying image is one of dryness and aridity: a dry branch is drained of its sap, dried out by the sun, and thus lifeless. This creates an image of fragility and death.
G5434.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning 'to dry up' or 'to scorch.' It evokes the action of fire and sun that deprives the plant of all moisture. In the Hebrew of the Greek Old Testament, it mostly translates the word קַשׁ (qash), which means straw or the dry residues of harvests — material of no value, good only for burning.
G5434.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:3, during the shipwreck of Paul and his companions on the island of Malta. Paul, to warm himself and make a fire, gathers dry branches he finds on the shore. This is a very concrete detail: on a Mediterranean island, dead wood accumulates on the shores and burns quickly. The context shows that the fire revives the nest of a viper hidden in this dry wood, leading to the dramatic incident that follows.
G5434.portee: This word reminds us that Paul, even in a situation of distress (shipwrecked, wet, cold), remains active and resourceful: he does not remain inert but seeks to survive. The detail of the dry branch also illustrates how God allows trials to come upon His faithful servants — here, the viper coming out of the dry wood — but miraculously delivers them (the viper does not truly harm him, despite the bite).

sens: historical region of Asia Minor
territory traversed by Christian missionaries in the early centuries
G5435.detail:
1. Phrygia is a region located in Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey, known in antiquity. At Pentecost, inhabitants of this region were present in Jerusalem (Acts 2:10) among the Jewish pilgrims who came from various parts of the Roman world.
2. During his missionary journeys, the Apostle Paul travels through Phrygia, often associated with the neighboring Galatia. In Acts 16:6 and 18:23, these two regions are mentioned together as territories that Paul traverses to strengthen the churches and proclaim the Gospel to the new Christian communities that have formed there.
G5435.origine: The name comes from the ancient Greek 'Phrygia' (Φρυγία), designating a well-identified historical region. In Hebrew and in the texts of the Old Testament, the same regions are often referred to by general geographical terms. The name 'Phrygia' recalls an ancient people, the Phrygians, who inhabited there.
G5435.emploi: The word 'Phrygia' appears three times in the Acts of the Apostles. In Acts 2:10, it is listed among the regions from which the pilgrims present at Pentecost came. In Acts 16:6 and 18:23, it is the scene of Paul's missionary activities, who travels through this region with his colleagues to visit and encourage the believers. The repeated mention of Phrygia emphasizes the expansion of early Christianity in Asia Minor.
G5435.portee: Phrygia reminds us that from the earliest days of the Church, the Gospel spread far beyond Jerusalem and that Paul, with zeal, traveled to distant regions to build up new churches. It is a testimony to the constant missionary activity and apostolic concern for young communities.

sens: Man of the apostolic era who abandoned the apostle Paul
G5436.detail: Phygelus is a Christian mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 1:15. Paul, writing to his young disciple Timothy from his prison in Rome, sadly reminds him that all those in Asia have abandoned him — and he specifically names Phygelus alongside Hermogenes as a striking example of this desertion. This is a serious act: at a time when Paul is suffering for the Gospel, Phygelus and others chose to turn away from him, likely fearing the consequences of remaining loyal to a jailed apostle who was judged as a criminal by Rome.
