G5436.origine: The name Phygelus comes from the Greek « phuge » (flight): it literally means « the one who flees ». It is a melancholic irony that this man bears a name evoking flight, and that he illustrated it by abandoning Paul at the moment when he needed support the most.
G5436.emploi: Phygelus appears only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Timothy 1:15. Paul mentions his name in a pastoral letter addressed to Timothy shortly before his death, in a context of loneliness and suffering. The fact that Paul explicitly names him, along with Hermogenes, shows that this defection deeply affected him — it is not a vague criticism, but a personal reproach against those who betrayed his trust in a dark hour. Nothing else is said about Phygelus in Scripture.
G5436.portee: Phygelus reminds us of a difficult reality taught throughout the Bible: that faithfulness to Christ and His Gospel can come at a high cost, and that some will retreat out of fear or personal interest. His example invites the reader to examine their own steadfastness: will we be faithful to God even when it becomes dangerous or unpopular? Paul himself, despite this pain, does not cease to serve — this is why his testimony contrasts with that of Phygelus and calls us to faithfulness.

sens: action of fleeing quickly from danger
hasty and involuntary departure from a place
G5437.detail:
1. Flight refers to the action of fleeing quickly from a threat: running away to escape danger. In Matthew 24:20, Jesus speaks of the flight of believers when armies surround Jerusalem — a forced and urgent retreat, not a mere departure.
2. The word also evokes the state of one who must leave quickly, without being able to stay or prepare: Jesus asks the disciples to pray that this flight « does not happen in winter, nor on a Sabbath day », meaning at a time that would make it even more difficult and perilous.
G5437.origine: The word φυγή (phugē) comes from the verb φεύγω (pheugō), « to flee ». In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word מָנוֹס (manōs, refuge in fleeing) and related forms for this meaning. The root evokes the action of escaping hastily, of fleeing to save oneself.
G5437.emploi: The word φυγή appears twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew and Mark, in Jesus' eschatological discourse (Matthew 24:20 and Mark 13:18). Jesus warns His disciples that the fall of Jerusalem would force believers into an urgent flight. He urges them to pray that this moment does not occur in winter (when traveling is difficult) nor on the Sabbath day (when movement was restricted by law). This is a real, material flight imposed by persecution and war, not a spiritual figure.
G5437.portee: This word reminds the disciples that they may sometimes have to leave everything to save themselves in the face of persecution — a reality that early Christians experienced. But Jesus also invites confident prayer: even in urgency and danger, God does not abandon us, and we can ask Him that the circumstances be as favorable as possible.

sens: Place where prisoners are confined
Group of guards or sentinels keeping watch
Action of monitoring, guarding something or someone
Division of the night during which guards ensure surveillance
G5438G.detail:
1. Prison is the building where detainees are held: this is the most common meaning in the New Testament. Jesus speaks of visiting those who are in prison (Matthew 25:43), and several disciples were imprisoned for their faith — Peter is freed from prison by divine intervention (Acts 12:17), and Paul recounts how he himself imprisoned the early Christians (Acts 22:4).
2. The word also refers to the guards themselves, those who keep watch and maintain order: this is the meaning of the Latin custodia. In Jerusalem, the apostles miraculously freed are found in the temple, while the guards were searching for them (Acts 5:25).
3. By extension, phulakē can mean the very act of guarding, monitoring something or someone — the work of one who ensures protection.
4. In the nighttime context, a « watch » or « vigil » refers to one of the four divisions of the night during which sentinels take turns to keep watch (Matthew 14:25: Jesus walks on the sea at the fourth watch).
G5438G.origine: The word comes from the verb phulassō, « to guard, protect ». Its basic image is that of active protection: watching over a place or person to defend them. In Hebrew, it is mostly found for mishmeréth (« guard, surveillance ») and related forms. The word family also includes phulax (« guard ») and phulássō (« to guard »), all linked to the idea of vigilance and protection.
G5438G.emploi: The word appears about 40 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. The meaning of « prison » overwhelmingly dominates (about 36 occurrences): this is where John the Baptist is imprisoned (Matthew 14:10), where the apostles are thrown (Acts 5:19), where the disciples expect to be led (Luke 22:33). Jesus speaks of it at the Last Judgment as a place where He went to visit the detainees (Matthew 25:36-44), showing the moral importance of this visit. Paul suffers imprisonment repeatedly (2 Corinthians 6:5; 11:23). The meaning of « guard » or « nighttime watch » appears in storm narratives and nighttime surveillance (Matthew 14:25; Mark 6:48; Luke 12:38).
G5438G.portee: This word reveals how the Bible views the suffering of prisoners: not as forgotten beings, but as men and women worthy of compassion and visitation (Matthew 25). For early Christians, imprisonment becomes a trial of faithfulness common to many disciples. The repeated mention of prison also shows the power of God as liberator: Peter comes out of prison not by escape, but by divine intervention (Acts 12), giving the reader assurance that God sees and acts even in the most closed places.

sens: Division of the night into periods of guard
Specific moment of the night when one stands guard
State of sustained attention, vigilance
G5438H.detail:
1. The night was divided into several periods called "watches," similar to the duration of a quarter of an hour of work: each corresponded to a few hours, and soldiers or guards would take turns to ensure surveillance. Jesus walks on the sea "in the fourth watch of the night" (Mark 6:48), meaning just before dawn, when the last watch was on duty.

2. The word also refers to each of these specific time slots: a night consisted of three or four "watches" depending on customs, and the Bible numbers them to indicate the exact moment. In Luke 12:38, Jesus says that the master may return "in the second or third watch."

3. By extension, a "watch" means being alert, remaining aware and attentive: the shepherds of Bethlehem "kept watch over their flocks by night" (Luke 2:8), meaning they stayed vigilant all night to protect their sheep.
G5438H.origine: The word comes from the verb meaning "to keep," "to watch over." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word for the same notion of night watch and surveillance. The root evokes the idea of protection: the one who stands guard ensures that nothing threatens.
G5438H.emploi: The Bible uses this word mainly in the Gospels to describe the division of the night into periods of guard (Matthew 14:25, Mark 6:48, Luke 12:38), a common military and civil practice. The shepherds in Luke 2:8 "kept watch over the night" while guarding their flocks, showing that nighttime vigilance was not reserved for soldiers. Jesus uses this vocabulary of night watch to speak of being ready for His return: those who remain vigilant, like attentive servants, will be "blessed" (Luke 12:38). The word expresses both a technical division of time and the spiritual attitude it symbolizes.
G5438H.portee: When Jesus speaks of the "watches," He transforms a detail of daily life into an image of spiritual vigilance. Remaining attentive "at every watch" means being ready at any moment, not falling asleep in indifference. For the Christian, this word reminds us that heart vigilance is never trivial: it is the attitude of one who awaits the Lord with seriousness and love.

sens: To throw someone in prison, to put them under guard
To deprive someone of freedom as punishment or forced detention
G5439.detail: 1. To imprison means to throw a person in prison, that is, to confine them by force behind bars or in a place of confinement, under the supervision of guards. Paul uses this word when he recounts to his accusers that, in the past, he would imprison those who believed in Jesus in the synagogues (Acts 22:19), which shows the brutality of his previous persecution. 2. Figuratively, the word can evoke any forced deprivation of freedom, any imposed confinement—whether physical or moral. It is a violent and authoritarian act, an instrument of repression.
G5439.origine: The word comes from the Greek phulakē (φυλακή), which means guard or prison, itself derived from the root phulassō (to guard, to watch over). The verb phulakizō adds the verbal suffix -izō to the noun phulakē, creating an active verb meaning "to put under guard" or "to imprison." The family of words revolving around guarding and surveillance is very rich in biblical Greek.
G5439.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 22:19), in Paul's speech before the crowd in Jerusalem. Paul confesses his past there: before his conversion, he actively imprisoned Christians in the synagogues, beat them with rods, and even sought to condemn them to death. This word shows the concrete reality of the persecution he waged against the early Church. Its unique use underscores the importance of this personal testimony of repentance and transformation.
G5439.portee: This word reminds Paul and every reader of the price that early Christians paid for their faith—imprisonment, violence, threat of death. For Paul himself, confessing this past is an act of radical humility: the one who imprisoned believers has become a prisoner of Christ himself. This challenges today's Christian regarding the reality of persecution and the transformative power of encountering Jesus.

sens: Small case containing passages of the written Law
Religious amulet or talisman worn for protection
External symbol of piety without heart commitment
G5440.detail:
1. A phylactery is a small leather strap or case that is attached to the body, particularly on the forehead or arm, to keep portions of Scripture. Among the Jews of Jesus' time, it was a religious practice based on texts like Exodus 13:16, where Moses commands to keep the Law "as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes." Pious men would therefore wear these small boxes that contained scrolls written with the divine commandments.
2. The word phylactery comes from a Greek root meaning "to guard" or "to protect": it is an object worn as a spiritual safeguard, a religious talisman meant to protect the wearer and constantly remind them of their duty to God.
3. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus criticizes the religious leaders who wear "large phylacteries" to be seen by men. He denounces not the object itself, but its abuse: these men made it an instrument of pride and vanity instead of a sincere aid to devotion, transforming a sign of piety into pure ostentation.
G5440.origine: The Greek word "phylactérion" derives from "phylax" (guardian) and "phulassô" (to guard, to protect). It literally designates a means of protection or a guard. In Hebrew, the corresponding object is called "tefillin" (לִלִּין), whose name comes from a root meaning "to pray." The Greek word was chosen to convey the concept to Greek readers: the emphasis shifts from prayer to protection, reflecting how the Greeks understood this Jewish practice as a form of apotropaic talisman.
G5440.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 23:5, in a discourse by Jesus against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and scribes. It is at this precise moment that Jesus enumerates the faults of these masters of the Law: they make large phylacteries and long fringes to impress the people. The context shows that the problem is not the practice itself (which was legitimate), but its diversion for the purposes of vanity and human recognition. Jesus denounces the proud heart that hides behind the appearance of external piety.
G5440.portee: This passage calls us to examine ourselves: do we wear external signs of religion to be seen and admired by others, or do our actions stem from an authentic relationship with God? Jesus teaches us that true piety is first lived in the secret of the heart, not on the front stage. It is a timeless warning against pharisaism, the gap between religious appearance and spiritual reality.

sens: Soldier or agent responsible for monitoring a place
Person who ensures the safety of a prisoner or a location
G5441.detail:
1. A guard is a soldier or security agent who monitors a strategic location or a prisoner. In Acts, guards are posted at the prison doors to prevent inmates from escaping (Acts 5:23; 12:6). It is a role of active and responsible surveillance.
2. The word also broadly refers to anyone tasked with protecting someone or something by constantly watching over it. Herod interrogates the guards after Peter's miraculous escape (Acts 12:19), as they were responsible for the prisoner's security with their lives.
G5441.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb φυλάσσω (phulassō), which literally means to watch over something or someone to preserve it from danger. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates שָׁמַר (shamar), the same verb God uses when He 'guards' His people. Thus, a guard is one who exercises this protective vigilance.
G5441.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Acts of the Apostles (5:23; 12:6; 12:19), in the account of Peter's miraculous release from prison. It specifically refers to Roman soldiers or security agents stationed at the prison. In all cases, these guards are tasked with ensuring that the prisoners do not escape; this is why Herod threatens them with death after Peter's escape. The usage is therefore always concrete and military, never figurative.
G5441.portee: This story of powerless guards in the face of Peter's miraculous release shows that no human surveillance, no matter how strict, can hinder God's action. The guards remind the reader that even earthly powers, including Herod and Rome, do not control the fate of God's servants. This is a source of encouragement for the persecuted.

sens: Watch carefully over someone or something to protect it or prevent it from escaping
Observe a law, command, or word by putting it into practice
Preserve, maintain intact a entrusted thing
Take care, be on guard against something
G5442G.detail:
1. To keep means primarily to watch over someone or something vigilantly, like a shepherd keeps his sheep or a guard keeps his prison. It is an active and constant responsibility. Example: in Luke 2:8, shepherds keep watch over their flocks at night ('were keeping watch').

2. To keep a law, word, or command means to put it into practice, to faithfully respect it. It is not merely knowing them, but living according to them. The rich young man in Matthew 19:20 claims to have 'kept' the commandments since his youth — he has implemented them. Jesus in John 12:47 speaks of those who 'keep' His word, meaning they receive it and live it.

3. To keep something can also mean to preserve, to maintain intact what has been entrusted to you. It is a notion of faithfulness towards a responsibility or a precious deposit.

4. In the middle voice (to keep oneself), the word expresses defensive vigilance: to take care, to be on guard against danger, as one guards against a trap.
G5442G.origine: The verb comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of watchfulness and protection. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates the verb שׁמר (shamar), which means to keep, observe, preserve — very often used for the observance of God's Law and covenants. This Hebrew root is at the heart of Israelite spirituality: to keep is to remain faithful to the Lord's commitments.
G5442G.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the provided usages, mainly in Luke, John, and Paul. It divides into two major uses. First, 'to keep' in the sense of conserving or protecting: to keep a person (Acts 12:4), a word (Luke 11:28). Secondly, and very frequently, 'to observe' in the sense of putting a law or command into practice: Matthew 19:20 and Mark 10:20 report that the young man 'kept' all the commandments since his youth; Acts 7:53 reproaches the Jews for not having 'kept' the Law received by the angels. Paul in Romans 2:26 and Galatians 6:13 mentions those who keep or do not observe legal prescriptions. The meaning nuances: to keep can be passive (to be kept) or active (to put into practice oneself), external (to observe a letter) or internal (to receive the meaning).
G5442G.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that the Law is not a dead weight, but a living responsibility to carry with vigilance. To keep God's word is not only to listen to it, but to live it — to integrate it into each day. For the reader of the New Testament, the word also reveals that Jesus Himself 'keeps' His disciples (John 17:12), protecting those entrusted to Him with divine vigilance. This transforms our understanding of obedience: it is not a servile submission, but a trust in the One who keeps us.

sens: Watch over someone to prevent them from escaping or to ensure their safety
Protect something or someone from danger or threat
Observe, respect a law, rule, command
G5442H.detail:
1. To keep means to closely monitor, to maintain under surveillance: it is to assign a guard or squad to watch over a detained or confined person, like the four squads that guarded Peter in prison (Acts 12:4) or the soldier who guarded Paul in Rome (Acts 28:16). This surveillance can also be passive, like that of the possessed man who was kept bound with chains (Luke 8:29).
2. To keep also means to defend, to preserve: it is the action of a strong man who keeps his house with his weapons, so that all he possesses remains protected and safe (Luke 11:21). It is an active vigilance against threats.
3. To keep a law, a command means to respect, to faithfully observe them — not only to know them, but to practice them. It is the attitude of the disciple or believer who strives to live according to God's will.
G5442H.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and primarily denotes the action of standing guard, watching over a place or person. In the Greek Scriptures, it often translates the Hebrew verb 'shamar' (שָׁמַר), which means to keep a flock, to hold someone in prison, as well as to observe a covenant or law. This richness of the Hebrew word explains that the Greek 'phulassō' covers all these meanings: to watch over, to protect, and to observe.
G5442H.emploi: The verb appears about 31 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. In Acts, it describes the concrete action of keeping a prisoner: Peter in Jerusalem, Paul on his way to Rome. In the Gospels, it also expresses protection (a strong man keeping his house) and the observance of commandments (the respect of the Law). In the epistles, particularly in Paul and Peter, it takes on a spiritual meaning: to keep the faith, to keep what has been entrusted, to guard against false doctrine. The meaning evolves from the concrete (physical surveillance) to the figurative (moral and spiritual vigilance).
G5442H.portee: This word calls the Christian to vigilance — not only to passively receive divine protection but also to respond with active obedience and a zealous guarding of the faith received. To keep God's word is to cherish and practice it; to keep one's heart is to remain on guard against anything that threatens the relationship with God. The word invites an active trust, where the believer becomes a guardian themselves, ensuring they remain faithful.

sens: To watch over, to keep an eye on someone or something to protect or maintain it safely
To protect someone from danger or evil
To preserve, to maintain in good condition
To observe, to respect a law, commandment, or rule
To guard against something, to take care to stay away from it
G5442I.detail:
1. To watch vigilantly: this is the image of shepherds watching over their flocks (Luke 2:8). The word evokes an active presence, a constant attention to ensure that nothing happens to the entrusted good.
2. To protect from danger or evil: Jesus says that he kept his disciples so that none would be lost (John 17:12), and Paul affirms that the Lord will preserve him from the evil one (2 Thessalonians 3:3). The image is that of an active defense against evil.
3. To keep intact, to maintain safely: Paul speaks of the deposit that he asks God to keep until the day of judgment (2 Timothy 1:12). The deposit is his faith or testimony; to keep it means to preserve it without alteration.
4. To respect and practice a law, a commandment: this meaning appears when speaking of keeping the Law or God's decrees (Acts 21:25). The word then means to obey and observe faithfully.
5. To guard against something: this is the reflexive meaning, to stay away from danger or what is forbidden (Luke 12:15, 2 Timothy 4:15). The image is that of someone who is careful, who takes care not to fall into temptation.
G5442I.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to close," "to enclose" — the basic idea is to put something under surveillance, to keep it within a guard or protection. In Greek, the word initially designated the action of watching over an area (a camp, a fortress) or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew שָׁמַר (shamar), which has exactly the same range of meanings: to watch, to protect, to observe. The family of the word includes terms like "guard" (the person or troop) and "prison" (the place where prisoners are kept).
G5442I.emploi: This verb appears 15 times in the given contexts, mostly in the epistles of the New Testament and in the Gospels. In the Gospels (Luke, John), it first designates the concrete action of watching (the shepherds) or protecting (Jesus keeping his disciples). In the epistles of Paul and Peter, the meaning broadens: to keep takes on a strong spiritual dimension (to keep the faith, to preserve one's deposit, to guard against evil). The passive form also appears ("to be kept," "to be preserved"), emphasizing that it is God who keeps us. The meaning of observing, respecting a law or commandment (Acts 21:25) shows that to keep also means to put into practice.
G5442I.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand that their protection comes from God, who "keeps" them from evil (2 Thessalonians 3:3). It also reminds that faith is not passive: one must "guard" against sin and error, watching over oneself with care. Finally, to "keep" a commandment means to live according to God's will, and it is in this that true security lies.

sens: a group of families united by a common ancestor and living together under a single authority
each of the twelve divisions of the people of Israel
a collective group of peoples or nations
G5443.detail:
1. A tribe is a human group where families are linked by blood and common habitation: it is like a large extended family that shares a territory and obeys the same leader. In the time of Israel, each tribe descended from one of Jacob's sons and bore his name — for example, the tribe of Benjamin from which Paul was descended (Philippians 3:5).
2. The term specifically refers to the twelve tribes of Israel, born from the twelve sons of Jacob. Jesus promises his apostles that they will sit on twelve thrones to judge these twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28). This is the religious and political heritage of God's people.
3. In Revelation, "tribe" expands to speak of all the peoples of the earth: when John sees the immense crowd worshiping the Lamb, it comes "from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation" (Revelation 5:9). The word then includes not only the descendants of Israel but all the peoples of the world.
G5443.origine: The Greek word φυλή comes from a root meaning "to grow" or "to produce": a tribe is primarily a lineage, a common descent. The Hebrew Old Testament used several words to express this idea — מַטֶּה (tribe) and שֵׁבֶט (staff, a symbol of a tribe's authority) — which the Greek version generally translates as φυλή. The word conveys both the blood relationship and the political bond of the group.
G5443.emploi: The word "tribe" appears 23 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. In the Gospels, it refers to the historical twelve tribes of Israel: Jesus promises that his disciples will judge them (Matthew 19:28 and Luke 22:30), and Paul claims descent from the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5). Revelation carefully lists the 144,000 elect coming from each tribe (Revelation 7:4-8), thus recalling the heritage of the chosen people. But the word also universalizes: in the vision of Revelation 5:9, "tribe" becomes a generic term for all the peoples who worship the Lamb, showing that salvation extends far beyond Israel. It is a shift from the particular (the chosen people) to the universal (all nations).
G5443.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Church inherits the promise made to Israel and that it is built on the twelve apostles as on twelve spiritual tribes. It also shows that God's plan encompasses all the peoples of the earth: salvation in Christ is not limited to any nation or group, but is addressed to every tribe in the world.

sens: The flat green part of a tree or plant
A visible sign of the life or growth of a plant
A promise of fruit that remains unfulfilled
A means of healing or well-being
G5444.detail:
1. The leaf is the flat green part that a tree or plant bears. This is what Jesus sees on the fig tree in Matthew 21:19, a covering of greenery that gives the impression that the tree is fertile.
2. The leaf is the sign that the plant is growing and alive. When leaves grow on the branches of the fig tree, it is the signal that summer is approaching (Matthew 24:32), like a promise of what is to come.
3. Sometimes the leaf deceives: it promises fruit, but the fruit is lacking. The fig tree in Mark 11:13 has leaves but no figs, revealing its sterility.
4. In the vision of heaven, the leaves of the tree of life have a virtue: they heal the nations (Revelation 22:2), they are no longer just an ornament but a remedy.
G5444.origine: The Greek word φύλλον comes from a root that expresses the idea of something that spreads or unfolds. In Hebrew, the word עָלֶה (ale) refers to both the individual leaf and the foliage of a tree. The word is simple and ancient in both languages, designating one of the most visible realities of living nature.
G5444.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels and Revelation. Three passages speak of the fig tree: two in Matthew (21:19 and 24:32) and two in Mark (11:13 and 13:28), as the lesson of the barren fig tree recurs in Jesus' teaching. Only one passage departs from this image: Revelation 22:2, where the leaves of the tree of life have a healing function. The leaf always appears as a concrete detail that reveals something deeper: the state of the tree, the season, or in the heavenly vision, the power of healing.
G5444.portee: The leaf reminds us that visible signs are not enough: an appearance of life or fertility can hide sterility. Jesus uses it as a moral lesson about the authenticity of the heart. But the image of the healing leaves of the tree of life also opens us to hope: in heaven, what grows on the divine tree is no longer deceptive, but truly brings salvation and restoration.

sens: Malleable substance obtained by mixing and working flour with water
Portion of soft and compact material, like the potter's clay
What can be shaped or transformed, an image of the community of believers
Subtle influence that extends to the whole, like yeast in dough
G5445.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the concrete dough obtained by kneading flour with water. It is a soft, worked substance, ready to be baked. Paul uses it to speak of the yeast that causes "the whole batch" to rise (1 Corinthians 5:6).
2. It also applies to a mass of inert and malleable material, like clay in the hands of the potter who shapes it into different vessels (Romans 9:21). The image is one of molding.
3. Figuratively, the community of believers is compared to this dough: the "firstfruits" (the first converts) sanctify "the whole mass" (Romans 11:16). The idea is that the whole is consecrated by its firstfruits.
4. The yeast in the dough illustrates how a small moral or doctrinal influence can extend to the entire community. A "little yeast" corrupts "the whole batch" (Galatians 5:9), just as the malice of a few threatens the purity of all.
G5445.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "knead, mix" and denotes the concrete result of this action. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the term "leavened dough" (שְׁאַר) is translated by this Greek term in the Old Testament translated into Greek. The image is always that of a soft, mixed, hand-worked material, capable of being transformed or undergoing transformation. It is a word from everyday language, without particular religious connotation at first.
G5445.emploi: This word appears five times in the New Testament, always in the Pauline epistles and with two main images. First, dough in the culinary sense: Paul uses it to warn the Corinthians against sin that contaminates the community, just as yeast causes the dough to rise (1 Corinthians 5:6-7; Galatians 5:9). Secondly, molded clay: the potter shapes his dough into vessels of different statuses, an image of divine sovereignty over creatures (Romans 9:21). Thirdly, the mass of the community: Paul says that if the firstfruits (first fruits) are holy, the whole mass is also (Romans 11:16). In each case, the word emphasizes either the influence that affects the whole or the capacity of the whole to be transformed or judged.
G5445.portee: For the Christian, this word teaches two major truths. On one hand, it reveals the absolute sovereignty of God: the Creator shapes like the potter, and each creature has value only in His design. On the other hand, it warns of the insidious power of sin: a little yeast — a tolerance towards evil, a doctrinal compromise — contaminates the entire community. It is a call to guard the collective purity of God's people, knowing that each one affects the whole.

sens: Produced by nature, innate
In accordance with nature, according to the natural order
Governed solely by natural instinct, without reason
G5446.detail:
1. The word refers to what is produced or given by nature itself, without artificial intervention — it pertains to the inherent constitution of a creature. In Romans 1:26-27, Paul speaks of the "natural use" of a woman, meaning what corresponds to the natural function that God has established.
2. More broadly, "natural" means what is in accordance with the natural order, the law of nature — in opposition to what is "against nature." This meaning predominates in Paul when he denounces passions against nature: he judges by the criterion of the created order.
3. The word can also qualify what pertains solely to instinct, without reason or conscience. In 2 Peter 2:12, people are compared to "brute beasts made to be caught," meaning creatures given over to their only natural inclinations, incapable of moral discernment — they act like mere animals.
G5446.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "physis" (φύσις), which means nature, essence, organic growth. It conveys the idea of what is born and develops according to its own internal law. The adjective "natural" thus describes what pertains to this nature, what arises from it or conforms to its laws. This root has given rise to the French words "physique" and "physiology." In classical Greek, the word often opposes what is artificial, acquired, or against nature.
G5446.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. In Romans 1:26-27, Paul uses it twice to refer to the natural use in the realm of sexuality, which he opposes to what transgresses the created order. In 2 Peter 2:12, it applies to creatures governed solely by instinct — this passage compares false teachers to animals, highlighting their moral degradation: instead of living according to reason and conscience, they act like beasts. In each case, the word refers to an objective criterion: the order established by creation.
G5446.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that the Bible recognizes a natural order intended by God and inscribed in creation. It is not an arbitrary moralistic judgment: it is a call to live in harmony with what God has established. For Paul, ignoring or violating this natural order is to rebel against the wisdom of the Creator Himself. This notion invites every believer to respect creation and its laws, not out of mere conformity, but out of obedience to the God whose wisdom has ordered everything.

sens: In a manner conforming to nature, instinctively
According to the natural order of things, without reflection or will
By animal instinct, like a beast
G5447.detail:
1. The word refers to what is done according to the inherent nature of a creature, without learning or conscious choice. In Jude 1:10, false teachers "corrupt themselves in what they know naturally": like animals acting purely on instinct, they follow their carnal impulses without resistance.
2. It is the opposite of what comes from the Spirit or true knowledge: while the Christian can dominate his nature by faith, the one who acts "naturally" remains enslaved to his animal desires, incapable of moral discernment.
G5447.origine: The word comes from the Greek physis ("nature"), with the suffix -ōs which makes it an adverb. It literally denotes the action "in the manner of nature." In biblical thought, acting "naturally" can be good when it involves creation obeying its laws, but it becomes bad when man, created in the image of God, refuses the light of his conscience and the call of God to remain at the level of animal instinct.
G5447.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:10. It describes the moral corruption of the ungodly who, willfully ignoring spiritual truth, follow their carnal appetites like beasts without reflection. It is a severe diagnosis: these men have lost the capacity for moral judgment and act purely on bestial instinct, without awareness of good and evil.
G5447.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian is called to transcend his natural instincts. Remaining at the level of "natural" reactions — anger, envy, covetousness — is to remain animalistic. Faith invites us to live according to the Spirit, which judges, discerns, and masters the impulses of the body. Willfully ignoring the truth of God to follow one's desires is to degrade oneself below one's human vocation.

sens: To inflate, to physically swell like with a bellows
To make proud, to instill a sense of pride
To be swollen with pride, to be filled with excessive arrogance
G5448.detail:
1. The word comes from the Greek "bellows": it describes the action of inflating something by filling it with air, as one would swell a wineskin or a balloon. This is the physical sense of the word.
2. Figuratively, it means to make someone proud or puffed up with pride. Knowledge, for example, "puffs up" those who possess it, filling them with excessive self-confidence (1 Corinthians 8:1).
3. To be swollen with pride is to be filled with an arrogance that distorts judgment and heart. In Corinth, some "were puffed up" thinking that Paul would not confront them, or because they tolerated a serious sin (1 Corinthians 4:18; 5:2). It is a state of spiritual swelling analogous to physical swelling: unreasonable, visible, contrary to the true nature of love (1 Corinthians 13:4).
G5448.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek "phusa" which literally means "bellows" — the tool with which air is blown. Hence the image of swelling or inflating. In classical Greek, the verb "physaō" had this direct sense: to fill with air. The Bible uses it exclusively in a figurative sense, to describe the swelling of the soul by pride, transforming the physical image into a moral one: just as a swollen body is deformed and sick, a soul swollen with pride is corrupted and malevolent.
G5448.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, always in Paul, concentrated in the first letter to the Corinthians (6 occurrences). In Corinth, pride was a plague: some believers were puffed up with knowledge (8:1), others with their supposed spiritual superiority (4:6, 4:18-19), and the entire community was swollen with pride in the face of the sin it tolerated (5:2). Paul uses the same word when he describes charity: it "does not puff up with pride" (13:4), which means that true love remains humble and is not inflated by pride. In Colossae, Paul warns against those who "are puffed up" with pride by their human ideas (Colossians 2:18). The word always paints a state of excessive swelling — an arrogance that blinds.
G5448.portee: This word reveals a spiritual danger often invisible: the pride that swells silently in the heart, especially when one possesses certain gifts or knowledge. Paul opposes it to charity and humility. Understanding this image of swelling helps the Christian recognize this inflation of pride within themselves and to ask God for true edifying charity, which does not inflate anyone.

sens: What constitutes the essence of a person or thing, its inherent characteristics
The origin, the condition of birth of someone
The regular and spontaneous order of things, what happens instinctively without learning
What is in accordance with this established order, the normal course of things
G5449.detail:
1. Nature is what makes a thing or person what it is — its characteristic traits, its essential properties. The nature of animals is their particular temperament (James 3:7). The nature of a person is how they are made, their essence (Ephesians 2:3: "children of wrath by nature" means that we are born, by our human condition, destined for divine wrath).

2. Nature can simply refer to where someone comes from, their condition of birth or race. An uncircumcised person "by nature" (Romans 2:27) is someone who was born without circumcision, who has never been circumcised by their origin. This describes someone's natural condition at birth.

3. Nature is also the regular, spontaneous, instinctive order of things — what happens naturally, without being taught. The pagans "do by nature" what the law prescribes (Romans 2:14): their conscience naturally inspires them to certain just acts, without having been taught. Nature itself teaches (1 Corinthians 11:14) that it is a shame for a man to have long hair.

4. "According to nature" or "against nature" refers to what is in accordance with or contrary to the established order of things. The "natural" branches of the olive tree (Romans 11:24) are those that belong to it naturally, by their creation. To act "against nature" (Romans 1:26) is to go against the order that God has established in the world.
G5449.origine: The word comes from the Greek phusis, derived from a root meaning "to generate, to push." Its primary image is that of growth, of what develops naturally. In common Greek, nature is what characterizes beings and things, what is inscribed in them since their birth. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it translates Hebrew terms also designating essence and order of things.
G5449.emploi: The word appears 11 times mainly in Paul's epistles, and in James and Peter. Paul uses it to speak of what is natural, by birth (Galatians 2:15: "we, Jews by nature"), to describe God's created order (animals have their own nature, Romans 11:21-24 with the natural or unnatural branches of the olive tree). He also uses the adverb "naturally" to describe what happens without teaching (Romans 2:14: pagans act naturally according to the law). It is especially in Romans 1 and 11 that "against nature" takes on a moral and theological force: Paul contests God's created order, the "natural" use that God has established. In 1 Peter 1:4 and James 3:7, nature refers to the essential qualities of created things and beings.
G5449.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that God has established a natural order in creation — in bodies, relationships, instincts — and that violating this order has serious consequences (Romans 1:26-27). It also reminds us that human conscience, even without the revealed Law, can discern what is right "naturally" (Romans 2:14), for God has engraved something in us. Finally, it shows that God's grace often operates against "nature": it transforms us beyond what we are natively (1 Peter 1:4, speaking of God enriching our "nature").

sens: Swelling of self-esteem, internal inflation of vanity
Arrogance that swells from within oneself
G5450.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of something that swells, that inflates — like a sail in the wind or a cheek that fills with air. It is the proud person who "swells" with themselves, filled with a high opinion of themselves. Paul speaks of this in Corinth: this "pride" (or this inflation of vanity) is a poison that adds to quarrels and jealousies, a disease of the soul that paralyzes it.
2. It is an active pride, which seeps through tone, gaze, words — an arrogance that is visible, that hurts, that divides. In Paul, this word comes up directly linked to the internal conflicts of the Church: pride is never alone; it brings discord with it.
G5450.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to swell" or "to inflate" (φυσάω). The same root produces "φυσιόω," which means "to fill with pride" or "to puff up." The basic image is that of air filling, dilating, swelling — a bodily image for a spiritual reality: pride is what "dilates" the soul in an unhealthy way, cutting it off from others and from God.
G5450.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:20. Paul lists the faults that risk defiling the Church and preventing his visit from bearing fruit: quarrels, jealousies, animosities, factions, slander, calumnies, and this "pride." It is a serious word, a spiritual diagnosis: pride is at the heart of the list of evils that fragment the body of Christ. Paul uses it only here to qualify it with particular force — it is a swelling of the soul that divides and destroys.
G5450.portee: For the believer, this word is a mirror: it shows how pride is never a solitary defect, but the seed of a multitude of sins — jealousy, rivalry, slander. Recognizing this "pride" within oneself is to see that our heart has "swelled" far from God and that we must renounce this vanity for the Church to breathe and for the Spirit to act.

sens: What has been planted, cultivated
Vegetation, grass or any tree
Figuratively: what is rooted, established
G5451.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of planting, the establishment of a plant in the ground — but also the result of this action, the plant itself, which has become alive and rooted. It conveys the idea of something living that grows and gradually takes root.
2. A plant is therefore simply a piece of vegetation, whether grass or tree, something that grows naturally from the soil. In Matthew 15:13, Jesus mentions "every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted."
3. Figuratively, the word carries the idea of what is established, rooted, destined to last or to perish according to its source. A plant "planted by the Father" is a durable and authentic spiritual reality; a plant "that the Father has not planted" will be uprooted, that is, rejected.
G5451.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb φυτεύω (phutéō, to plant). The root evokes the vital action of making something grow, transplanting, rooting something. In Hebrew, this same semantic field is found in the words נָטַע (neṭà', to plant) and מַטָּע (matːà', plantation), which appear in the Old Testament to describe the action of cultivating or the result of that cultivation. The fundamental idea is one of growth and rooting.
G5451.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 15:13, in a teaching of Jesus about what is pure and impure. Jesus responds to a question from the disciples by stating that every plant which God has not planted will be uprooted. The spiritual context makes this concrete term a powerful image: a plant "from the Father" is something true and lasting, while a plant foreign to His action will be destroyed. The unique use of the word reinforces its impact: it is precisely this term that unites common agriculture and the spiritual reality of the Kingdom.
G5451.portee: This word from Jesus liberates the believer: what does not come from God, even if it appears established or important, will ultimately be uprooted. Conversely, it assures that what God has planted—His Word, His Church, His disciples—has deeply established roots. The disciple may ask: is my faith, my works, my community planted by God or by myself alone? This image of the plant calls for trust and examination of what has truly founded our spiritual life.

sens: To put a plant, a tree, a vine in the ground so that it grows
To establish or found something lasting
To entrust a task or responsibility to someone
G5452.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to plant is to insert a seed or a young tree into the ground for it to develop. The Lord's parable illustrates this image: "A man planted a vineyard" (Matthew 21:33) speaks of this foundational work. Jesus also uses this image to show the power of faith: "you would say to this sycamore: Be uprooted and planted in the sea" (Luke 17:6).

2. The verb takes on a figurative meaning when it comes to founding or establishing something that lasts. Jesus teaches that "every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted" (Matthew 15:13): He speaks here of what is truly established by God, as opposed to what comes from men alone. Paul uses this image for his apostolic work: "I planted; Apollos watered" (1 Corinthians 3:6-8), where to plant means to lay the foundation of faith in a heart.

3. Finally, the word denotes the action of entrusting a task or mission. When Paul speaks of one who "plants" a vineyard (1 Corinthians 9:7), he means one who has established it and has the responsibility for it, just as an employer entrusts a task to a worker.
G5452.origine: The word comes from φυτόν (phutón), "plant," which traces back to φύω (phúō), "to cause to grow, to produce." The root evokes the natural action of bringing forth life from the earth. In Hebrew, φυτεύω primarily translates נָטַע (nata'), "to plant," which has the same concrete and figurative meanings: to establish, to found, to implant durably.
G5452.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and Paul. In Luke, it describes concrete acts of ordinary life ("they planted, they built," Luke 17:28) or images from the parable of the fig tree (Luke 13:6). Matthew and Mark use the same verb in the parable of the vinedressers (Matthew 21:33; Mark 12:1). Paul systematically uses this image for his apostleship: he "plants" when he establishes a Christian assembly, Apollos "waters" (1 Corinthians 3:6-8), and God "gives the increase." This liturgical and missionary image shows how the apostle understands his role not as one who produces faith, but as one who sets it in place and provides the conditions for it to grow.
G5452.portee: This word teaches two precious truths for the Christian. First, that everything that lasts comes from God alone: what He has not planted will be uprooted, while His work stands firm. Second, that faith grows in stages, like a plant: some plant, others water, but only God gives the increase. The Christian on mission will find encouragement here: his role is not to accomplish everything alone, but to faithfully lay what God entrusts to him.

sens: To emerge from the ground, to grow (referring to a plant)
To produce, to generate (active sense)
To spring up, to rise spontaneously and threateningly
G5453.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning: a seed or plant that comes out of the ground and grows. In the parable of the sower (Luke 8:6, 8), the seed that falls on the rock or on good soil "rises" — it germinates and begins to grow. It is the image of life springing from the soil.
2. More broadly, "to produce" or "to generate": what brings something into being, notably offspring. The word can denote the action of giving birth.
3. Figuratively, to spring up or rise spontaneously and often dangerously: in Hebrews 12:15, a "root of bitterness" that "sprouts" — it germinates threateningly in the heart of a community, like a weed that spreads and contaminates.
G5453.origine: The verb comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of growth and production. It is related to words denoting nature, plant, biological growth. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it often translates the Hebrew word עָלָה (to go up, to rise), which shows that the image is one of ascent, of emergence from the ground.
G5453.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to express growth or germination. Two occurrences are found in the parable of the sower in Luke (8:6 and 8): they describe how the seed "rises" or "germinates" according to the quality of the soil. A third occurrence in Hebrews 12:15 uses the word figuratively: a root of bitterness that "sprouts" or "rises" — a hidden hostility that grows and manifests itself. The context is always one of emergence, of a surge of life or evil.
G5453.portee: This word invites us to meditate on growth — that of the seed of the Kingdom within us, but also that of the roots of bitterness or resentment that can spring up in our hearts. It reminds us that hidden attitudes eventually come to light and produce their effects: spiritual vigilance consists of stopping evil at its source, before it "grows" and spreads.

sens: Burrow or lair of a wild animal
Refuge, natural hiding place
G5454.detail:
1. A den is the burrow or lair that an animal digs or occupies for shelter and sleep. It is a hole, a cavity in the ground, or a cave: Jesus says that "foxes have dens" (Matthew 8:20), which evokes the underground shelters where these animals rest.
2. The word also more broadly designates a refuge, a natural hiding place where creatures retreat. Jesus uses this image to emphasize that he does not even have this simple refuge: unlike foxes and birds, which naturally possess a resting place, the Son of Man "has nowhere to lay his head" (Luke 9:58), illustrating his voluntary destitution.
G5454.origine: The Greek word φωλεός comes from a root expressing the idea of digging or making a hole. It literally designates the natural or dug hollow where a beast resides. The family of the word is limited in Greek, but the image is that of a dug or hidden refuge, a primary shelter.
G5454.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, solely in Jesus' discourse in Matthew 8:20 and its parallel in Luke 9:58. In these two parallel passages, Jesus contrasts the assured rest of wild animals with his own destitution: foxes have dens, birds have nests, but he, the Messiah, has nowhere to lay his head. This is not a complaint, but a prophetic statement of his condition as a rejected messenger. The context is that of the call to discipleship: following Jesus requires more renunciation than the harsh life of wandering animals.
G5454.portee: This image of the den reminds Christians that following Jesus involves destitution: he has not promised material comfort, but an intimate communion with him. It also invites a perspective of faith: if God provides for wild beasts, how much more will he provide for those who trust him, even without assured shelter.

sens: To shout, to speak loudly
To cry in a certain way (loud, piercing, joyful)
To address someone, to give an order
To summon someone, to bring them in
To give someone a name, to designate them by a title
G5455.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to shout or speak loudly so that one can be heard from afar. In Luke 8:8, Jesus speaks loudly a significant word that everyone must hear.

2. Sometimes the cry has a particular quality: it can be piercing and frightening (the cry of the demoniac in Mark 1:26), joyful (the disciples shout "Hosanna!"), or desperate (the thieves insult Jesus in Matthew 27:47).

3. When one "calls" someone, one publicly addresses them to come or to give them an order: Jesus calls the twelve in Mark 9:35, or the Samaritan woman calls her husband in John 4:16.

4. It is also to summon: one calls servants or guests to come (Luke 14:12, Luke 16:2).

5. Finally, this verb can mean "to designate someone by a name or title": the disciples call Jesus "Master and Lord" in John 13:13, meaning they recognize and name him as such.

6. For animals, particularly the rooster: the verb simply means "to sing" or "to cry" — the rooster crows in Matthew 26:34, Luke 22:34 (this is the signal that reminds Peter of his denial).
G5455.origine: The word comes from the root "phoné," which evokes the sound of the voice, noise, or speech. This root is found in "telephone" (to send the voice far away), "microphone," etc. In Hebrew, this verb often translates the word "קָרָא" (qara), which means "to cry, to call, to summon" — it is a cry or a call that wants to be heard. The Greek word "phōneō" has retained this idea of a voice that carries, that crosses space.
G5455.emploi: The verb appears 39 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in Acts. It is divided between two main uses: 1) to shout, to speak loudly — this is rare and mainly the cry of demons or the voice of Jesus proclaiming (Mark 1:26, Luke 8:8). 2) to call someone, to summon or to designate — this is the most common use. Jesus calls the sick, the disciples, the crowds (Mark 9:35, Luke 14:12, John 11:28). The disciples call Jesus by his title "Lord" (John 13:13). The rooster crows or "sings" — this is a special use, always in the passages of Peter's denial (Matthew 26:34, Luke 22:34). The use evolves slightly: first a simple cry or address, then a relationship of naming or recognition.
G5455.portee: This word reminds us that the voice has power: that of Jesus who calls (it is an act of power and choice) and that of the one who recognizes Jesus by calling him by his name or title. When one "calls" someone, one establishes them in a way — one recognizes them, places them in a relationship. It is also the meaning of the rooster's crow: a call, a signal, that awakens and brings back to reality.

sens: Sound produced by the throat and mouth of a person who speaks or shouts
Cry of a person in distress or indignation
Sound produced by a being or an inanimate object
Language, tongue, speech
Word understood as being that of God himself
Act of speaking, producing a perceptible sound
G5456G.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the sound of human speech: the noise that comes from the throat when one speaks, louder or softer depending on the effort. In Luke 9:35, a voice comes from the cloud proclaiming: "This is my chosen Son" — it is the sound of a divine word heard audibly. In Acts 14:10, Paul speaks "with a loud voice" so that the paralytic can hear him well.
2. A cry that expresses strong emotion: pain, a call for help, protest. In Matthew 2:18, we hear "cries" in Ramah — these are not ordinary words but lamentations. In Luke 8:28, the demoniac cries "with a loud voice" upon seeing Jesus, mixing fear and defiance.
3. The word also applies to sound produced by beings or inanimate things. In Hebrews 12:19, it speaks of the "noise" of the trumpet and the words at Sinai — the sound of the trumpet is called a voice because it is heard, distinguished, and conveys something. In Revelation 8:13, a voice of an eagle resounds in the sky, announcing calamities.
4. The word can designate the tongue itself, the manner of speaking of a people. In 1 Corinthians 14:10, Paul lists "so many languages" in the world — each is a different voice, a distinct speech.
5. When the voice is that of God, it carries absolute authority: it is not just a noise, but the expression of divine will. In John 12:28, the voice of the Father comes from heaven to glorify his name. In John 5:37, Jesus says that those who listen to him have heard "the voice" of the Father himself.
6. Finally, the word simply expresses the act of speaking, making oneself heard, producing a sound that can be received. In John 10:27, the sheep of Christ "hear his voice" — that is, they recognize him, they perceive and receive his words.
G5456G.origine: The Greek φωνή (phōnē) comes from a root that evokes the sound produced by the vocal cords, the noise that comes from the mouth. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew קוֹל (qol), which also means "voice" and "noise" — showing that in biblical thought, a voice is a significant sound, a noise that carries meaning or intention. The associated verb φωνέω (phōneō) means "to call, shout, speak aloud." The word family also includes φωνητής, which designates one who can express themselves.
G5456G.emploi: The word voice appears 114 times in the New Testament and covers a very wide range of uses. In the Gospels, it appears especially when reporting words spoken aloud, or when expressing the emotion of those who cry out: John the Baptist cries "with a voice" (Luke 3:4), the demoniacs cry (Mark 5:7, Luke 4:33), the crowd protests (Luke 23:23). The most solemn moments feature a voice from heaven: to Jesus in Matthew 3:17 and Mark 1:11, to the Father in John 12:28 — these divine voices come from heaven or from the cloud and proclaim what must be heard and believed. In Acts, the apostles preach "with a loud voice" (2:14, 14:10) so that all can hear. In the epistles, the voice becomes less concrete: in Hebrews, it is that of God who spoke in the past (3:7, 12:26). In 1 Corinthians 14, Paul discusses different voices, languages, as charisms of the Holy Spirit. Revelation multiplies the voices from heaven — voices of angels, voices of the Lord — each conveying a message or proclaiming glory.
G5456G.portee: For the believer, the voice of Christ is the sign by which he recognizes and follows him (John 10:27). Listening to the voice of God means receiving his word with obedience, not as a vague noise but as a personal and living call. The word reminds us that God addresses his people, that he speaks and makes himself heard — his word is not a distant abstraction, but a noise, a heard and living reality, that calls for a response.

sens: Sound produced by the speech of a person
Word or discourse of a person
Sound or noise produced by an inanimate object
Ability to speak or language
Sound or call coming from heaven, the divine
G5456H.detail:
1. Sound produced by the speech of a person: it is the sound that our throat produces when we speak. In Revelation 1:10, John hears "a loud voice, like the sound of a trumpet" — it is indeed an audible, vocal sound.
2. Word or discourse of a person: by extension, the word designates what is said, the content of the speech. It is the voice of someone addressing us, their message. John 5:37 speaks of "the voice of God," meaning what God says.
3. Sound or noise produced by an inanimate object: a trumpet, an instrument, the wind can also produce a "voice." John 3:8 says "you hear its sound" when speaking of the wind — the same Greek word is used to designate this natural noise.
4. Ability to speak or language: in 1 Corinthians 14:10, "there are many languages in the world," literally "many different voices." The word can mean the language one speaks, the way of expressing oneself.
5. Sound or call coming from heaven, the divine: in the Gospels and Revelation, a "voice from heaven" designates the direct intervention of God. Mark 1:11 reports a voice from heaven at the baptism of Jesus — it is God addressing directly.
G5456H.origine: The Greek word φωνή (phōnē) comes from a root that evokes the produced sound, the noise. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word קוֹל (qôl), which literally means "voice" but also "noise," "sound," "call." The word family includes the verb φωνέω (phonéō), "to call," "to make one's voice heard." The starting image is therefore that of vocal sound, of what is heard.
G5456H.emploi: The word φωνή appears about 140 times in the New Testament and is very frequent in Revelation. It primarily designates the spoken human voice: that of John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3), that of a woman (Luke 1:44). But it quickly expands to include inanimate sounds: Matthew 24:31 mentions "the resounding trumpet," literally "the voice of a trumpet." In 1 Corinthians 14:7, a flute "makes a sound." In Revelation, "voices" often accompany divine interventions (Revelation 8:5, 10:4, 16:18) — these are not always words, but audible manifestations of the divine. The word can therefore designate both a precise word and a simple noise, but always something that is heard.
G5456H.portee: In the Bible, the voice holds crucial importance: it is the means by which God communicates with man ("Listen to the voice of the Lord"). Hearing the voice of God or that of Jesus means receiving a personal call, a direction. This word reminds Christians that God does not remain silent — he speaks, he calls, he makes himself heard. The voice from heaven in Revelation symbolizes the irruption of the divine into history.

sens: Physical clarity, luminous radiation that allows one to see
Fire or flame that illuminates
Clarity, divine truth revealed
The presence and holiness of God
Teaching, spiritual understanding
The one who brings truth, particularly Christ
G5457.detail:
1. Natural light produced by the sun or a fire, which illuminates and allows for vision (Acts 9:3: a light shone from heaven around Paul on the road to Damascus).
2. Fire or flame of a lamp or hearth that illuminates a space (Luke 8:16: no one lights a lamp and puts it under a basket).
3. Truth and spiritual understanding opposed to the darkness of ignorance and lies (John 3:20: everyone who does evil hates the light, lest his deeds should be exposed).
4. The radiant presence of God, His glory and holiness that dwells in unapproachable light (1 Timothy 6:16: God dwells in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see).
5. Intelligence, discernment, spiritual knowledge received from God (Luke 11:35: take heed that the light which is in you is not darkness, referring to the state of spiritual understanding).
6. Person or function of one who reveals truth and guides others to God (Romans 2:19: you are confident that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness).
G5457.origine: The Greek word φῶς (phōs) comes from an ancient root φάω (phāō) which means to shine or to illuminate. This image of radiance and clarity has been naturally applied in the Greek Old Testament to divine light, particularly translating the Hebrew אוֹר (or). The notion progresses from the simple physical phenomenon to the spiritual reality of divine revelation and knowledge of God.
G5457.emploi: The word light appears 68 times in the New Testament with a particular concentration in John and the Pauline epistles. In the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it primarily refers to physical light or miraculous heavenly clarity during revelations. In John, the word becomes highly theological: light is one of the deepest divine realities, associated with the Word of God and the revelation of Christ. In 1 John 1:5, God Himself is described as light. In the Pauline epistles, the emphasis is on moral and spiritual light: those who believe become children of light and receive the fruit of light. The contrast between light and darkness structures the biblical symbolism of the opposition between good and evil, truth and lies, knowledge and ignorance, life and death.
G5457.portee: This word shows believers that God is not hidden or inaccessible: He desires His truth to be seen and known, just as light drives away darkness. Christians are called to be light in the world (Matthew 5:14), which commits them to live publicly in accordance with their faith and to reveal the Gospel through their conduct. Walking in the light means living in communion with God, accepting His revelation in Christ, and rejecting lies. It is an invitation to come out of spiritual darkness into the knowledge of God.

sens: Celestial body or star that emits light
Object that shines and illuminates, source of brilliant light
Figuratively: person who radiates, who shines through their testimony or virtue
G5458.detail:
1. In its most concrete sense, a torch is a celestial body — sun, moon, or star — that produces light in the sky. It is a luminous body that naturally illuminates the world.

2. More broadly, it refers to any object that shines and sparkles, any brilliant light source: a precious stone that glitters, a bright light that radiates. In Revelation 21:11, it speaks of the brilliance of a "very" precious stone, and the word suggests this quality of brightness and luminosity.

3. Figuratively, the torch becomes the image of the believer who shines through their conduct and testimony in the world. In Philippians 2:15, Paul calls Christians to shine "as lights" in a perverse generation: they are called to radiate virtue, purity, and spiritual light, visible to all.
G5458.origine: The word comes from the Greek phôs (light, clarity). A torch is literally that which carries or produces light. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew maor (luminary, celestial body) regarding the stars created on the fourth day, and zohar (splendor, brightness) to denote radiant brilliance. The family of this word encompasses all terms of light and brightness in Greek.
G5458.emploi: The word phōstēr appears only twice in the New Testament. In Philippians 2:15, Paul uses it figuratively to urge Christians to conduct themselves as torches shining in the moral darkness of the world — it is an image of positive influence and visible testimony. In Revelation 21:11, it describes the brilliance of a precious stone in the new heaven, where the luminous image returns to the more concrete sense of radiant splendor. In both cases, the word carries the idea of something that shines, sparkles, and stands out.
G5458.portee: This word reminds Christians that they are called to be a visible light in the world. Just as a torch cannot remain hidden, the faith and purity of the believer must shine evidently, so that others see their blameless conduct and glorify God. It is an invitation not to conform to the world, but to shine through holiness.

sens: The star that shines before the rising of the sun, the brightest of the fading night
Figuratively, that which brings light and hope in darkness
The divine promise that guides and illuminates the believer's heart
G5459.detail:
1. The morning star is literally the brightest star that appears just before dawn, when the night is still dark. It is Venus, also called the "evening star." In 2 Peter 1:19, it symbolizes the prophetic word that shines in the darkness of the world until the day dawns.
2. Figuratively, this term refers to anything that brings light and hope when darkness reigns. Peter compares prophecy to a lamp shining in a dark place, then to the morning star rising, suggesting a progression of clarity.
3. For the believer, the morning star represents the divine promise and the presence of Christ that illuminates the heart. It is the sign that the day is approaching, that the wait will end. It symbolizes the firm hope of the Christian in the coming of the Lord.
G5459.origine: The word comes from the Greek "phôs" (light) and "phérô" (to bear, to bring): literally "the one who brings light." It is an ancient poetic image, used by Greek philosophers. In Hebrew, there are equivalent expressions to designate Venus: the "morning star" that announces the dawn.
G5459.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:19. Peter uses it in a figurative and spiritual sense: he is not speaking of the astronomical body, but of the prophetic word that illuminates the faith of the believer. The image of the morning star rising in the heart (not in the sky) confirms this metaphorical sense. It evokes both the present light (the Scriptures read and meditated upon) and the future hope (the anticipation of the day of the Lord).
G5459.portee: For the believer, this image affirms that God's promises and His Word are a sure light in the present, even before the final glory. They do not leave the Christian wandering in the darkness of doubt or ignorance, but guide and assure them that the day is dawning. It is an invitation to base one's trust on the prophetic Scriptures until the coming of Christ.

sens: That which spreads or receives light
That which is clear, well visible
That which is purified, without inner darkness
G5460.detail:
1. This word describes what shines or emits natural light. The cloud that covers Jesus at His transfiguration is described as "luminous" (Matthew 17:5), radiant with the divine glory that is manifested there.

2. More broadly, luminous applies to what is clear and bright, capable of illuminating. The healthy eye is compared to a "lamp" that fills the whole body with light (Luke 11:34).

3. Figuratively, the word designates the inner state of a person: a purified heart, without areas of darkness or guilt. Jesus teaches that if "your whole body is full of light," with no part in darkness, then it will be entirely luminous (Luke 11:36). This is the biblical image of a clear conscience and a life fully placed under divine light.
G5460.origine: The word comes from the Greek phôs (light): it is a direct adjective formed simply to describe what belongs to light or has its nature. Phôs itself is one of the great biblical words: it evokes both physical light and truth, revelation, the presence of God. Luminous inherits this richness: it is to be on the side of divine light, opposed to darkness and gloom (skoteinós in Greek).
G5460.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Matthew or Luke. It is first used for physical realities: the luminous cloud of the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:5), or the eye that lets light in (Matthew 6:22 and Luke 11:34). But its usage quickly reveals a spiritual significance. The eye is not just an organ: it symbolizes intention, inner vision, the direction of the heart. A luminous eye makes a luminous body; a troubled eye plunges everything into darkness. Jesus uses this image to teach that moral and spiritual integrity — having a single gaze, a single intention — floods the entire life with clarity.
G5460.portee: This word invites the Christian to seek light not only outside but inside: that of a clear conscience, of a heart fully directed toward God. Jesus suggests that true light is not only received but lived — it transforms the one who bears it. To be luminous is to allow divine truth to penetrate every corner of one's inner life.

sens: To shine, give light (in the literal sense)
To illuminate, fill with light (physically)
To reveal, bring to light what was hidden
To instruct, provide spiritual understanding
G5461.detail:
1. The verb first describes the action of shining or giving light: it is the luminous radiance itself. In Revelation 22:5, the light of the Lord illuminates the redeemed eternally.
2. In a more concrete physical sense, it is to illuminate something or someone with light. In Luke 11:36, the lamp illuminates the whole body by spreading its light everywhere.
3. The meaning transfers to the moral and spiritual domain: to illuminate then means to reveal, to bring to light what was hidden or secret. In 1 Corinthians 4:5, the Lord will bring to light what was hidden in darkness, that is, expose what was secret.
4. Finally, in the realm of knowledge and faith, to illuminate means to provide understanding, to instruct, to enlighten the mind. In Ephesians 1:18, Paul prays that God will enlighten the eyes of the hearts of believers, that is, that He will give them to see and understand spiritual realities.
G5461.origine: The word comes from the Greek phôs (φῶς), which means "light." It is a verb formed on this root: literally, "to make light" or "to render luminous." The starting image is physical and concrete — the light that shines and illuminates the material world — but it is very early used in Greek as an image for intellect, knowledge, and understanding. In the Greek Bible, this verb often translates the Hebrew אוֹר (or, light) or Hebrew verbs meaning "to shine," "to illuminate," or "to reveal." The ecclesiastical Greek takes up this symbolic richness: to illuminate speaks of divine revelation.
G5461.emploi: The verb φωτίζω appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Pauline epistles and Revelation. In John 1:9, the true Light "illuminates every man who comes into the world" — here, to illuminate describes Christ's action toward humanity. In Paul, the word is frequent in a spiritual sense: in Ephesians 1:18 and 3:9, it is about enlightening the believer's understanding so that he may comprehend divine mysteries. In 1 Corinthians 4:5, it is to bring to light secrets. In 2 Timothy 1:10, it is to manifest life and immortality. Revelation also uses the word: in 21:23 and 22:5, God's light illuminates the heavenly city. Thus, the meaning varies from the literal to the spiritual, but always with the central idea that light reveals, exposes, and makes visible.
G5461.portee: This word speaks of God's revelation in two dimensions: that of the visible world (divine light fills heaven and earth) and that of the believer's soul. When we read that in Ephesians 1:18 God enlightens the eyes of the heart, we understand that faith is not primarily a matter of reason, but of inner illumination: God makes us see. This invites every Christian to ask God to open their understanding of the Scriptures and to dispel the darkness of their misunderstanding. It is also an encouragement: nothing remains hidden before God; He brings everything to light (1 Corinthians 4:5).

sens: Light that shines, illumination
Brightness, radiance
Clarity of knowledge or truth
Manifested glory, revelation of God
G5462.detail:
1. The word first designates light in the physical sense, the illumination that allows one to see — like the daylight that dispels darkness. In 2 Corinthians 4:6, Paul speaks of the light that God has "shone" in our hearts, an image of clarity and manifestation.
2. By extension, it is the brightness, the radiant glow of something glorious. In 2 Corinthians 4:4, it refers to the "splendor of the Gospel of the glory of Christ" — not just an ordinary light, but the radiant brilliance of divine revelation.
3. When it comes to knowledge or truth, this word evokes that inner clarity that allows one to understand and grasp reality. The heart becomes the seat of this spiritual illumination.
4. At the highest sense, it is the glory of God Himself that is manifested and unveiled — this inexhaustible brilliance of divine presence and power, particularly revealed in Christ.
G5462.origine: The word comes from the verb "to illuminate" (phōtizō), which means to shine light on something to make it visible. It is from the family of the Greek word that designates physical light. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "or" (light) and "mā'ôr" (source of light), which describe both created light and divine glory. The suffix changes the verb into an abstract noun, just as "to walk" becomes "walk."
G5462.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 4, by Paul. In 2 Corinthians 4:4, Paul uses it to describe the splendor of the Gospel that unbelievers do not see because their understanding has been blinded. In 2 Corinthians 4:6, he uses it to evoke the inner light that God produces in us, which illuminates our knowledge of the glory of God in Christ. In both cases, Paul contrasts clarity and spiritual illumination with blindness and darkness. It is a very theological word, related to the revelation and manifestation of God.
G5462.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Gospel is not obscure or secret, but a radiant splendor, a manifest glory — even if the world rejects it through blindness. It also shows that faith is not a blind belief, but an inner illumination of the heart, a clarity that God Himself produces in us to help us see the glory of Christ. It is an invitation to pray that God opens the eyes of our hearts to this light.

sens: To experience a lively joy, a delight
To take pleasure in something, to be glad about it
To welcome someone with kindness, to greet
To encourage one another to joy, to rejoice despite trials
G5463.detail:
1. To rejoice is to experience a deep and manifest inner joy. It is the happy emotion that seizes someone who receives good news or sees what they were waiting for come to pass. The Magi "were filled with very great joy" when they saw the star (Matthew 2:10): they rejoiced at discovering the sign they were seeking. It is also the joy of the father who sees his lost son return alive (Luke 15:32).

2. To rejoice in something is to be glad about it, to find it good that it has happened. Paul rejoices that the Philippians have renewed their feelings for him (Philippians 4:10). Jesus rejoices that Thomas will believe through the signs (John 14:28). It is a joyful adherence of the heart to what happens.

3. The word becomes a greeting: "Rejoice!" (or "Greetings!") welcomes someone with kindness and wishes them well. The angel says to Mary: "Rejoice, you who are highly favored" (Luke 1:28). The soldiers say to Jesus, "Rejoice, King of the Jews" (Matthew 27:29), ironic words that nonetheless remain a form of address.

4. To rejoice can also be a call to inner joy, an exhortation to exult despite circumstances. Jesus says: "Rejoice and leap for joy" (Luke 6:23) when you are persecuted. It is the Christian joy that persists beyond suffering.
G5463.origine: The verb χαίρω comes from a root expressing clarity, grace, and kindness. In Hebrew, it primarily translates שָׂמַח (samah, to rejoice) and גִּיל (gil, to exult). In Greek tradition, "to rejoice" is linked to the idea of moving from sorrow to joy, of finding grace. The family name χάρις (grace) comes from the same root: rejoicing and grace are sisters.
G5463.emploi: The verb χαίρω is one of the most common in the New Testament to express joy: 68 occurrences in total. Matthew, Luke, and John favor it in joyful events (Nativity, resurrection, reunions). Paul frequently uses it to exhort young churches to joy, notably in Philippians: "Rejoice in the Lord" (Philippians 3:1, 4:4). In the context of persecution (Acts 5:41), the verb emphasizes the paradoxical joy of disciples who are tormented. As a greeting, it opens official letters (Acts 15:23) or words of welcome. The meaning varies: emotional joy, intellectual adherence, moral exhortation, and simple formal courtesy.
G5463.portee: To rejoice teaches the Christian that joy is not a fleeting feeling attached to happy circumstances, but an attitude of the heart rooted in the relationship with God and His Lord. Even in tribulation, the believer can rejoice because their salvation is assured and their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). It also invites a kind courtesy towards others: greeting someone with a joyful heart is to welcome them as a child of light.
